11. Conclusion 
11.1 Reasoning Discipline as Governance Infrastructure 
This paper has argued that reasoning discipline is not a peripheral concern in AI-assisted 
governance, but a form of infrastructure in its own right. 
When AI systems are used to explain, analyze, or prepare governance materials, the way they 
reason becomes part of the governance environment — even when no execution or 
enforcement occurs. Without explicit boundaries, learning, operational analysis, and inspection 
reasoning can easily blur, creating ambiguity and misplaced confidence. 
Access-Mode is offered as a practical response to this reality. It does not introduce new 
authority or replace existing governance mechanisms. Instead, it provides a way to make 
reasoning posture visible, stable, and reviewable, so that AI assistance can be used without 
eroding accountability or interpretability. 
In this sense, reasoning discipline supports governance in the same way that clear roles, 
procedures, and documentation do: by making intent explicit and behavior understandable.

11.2 From Artifact Governance to Cognitive Governance 
Much of modern governance relies on carefully constructed artifacts — policies, standards, 
frameworks, and reports — that assume human judgment in their interpretation and use. 
As AI systems increasingly interact with these artifacts, a new layer of governance becomes 
necessary: not over the artifacts themselves, but over the cognitive processes applied to them. 
Access-Mode reflects a shift from focusing solely on what governance artifacts say, to also 
considering how reasoning about them occurs. This shift does not diminish the importance of 
artifacts. Rather, it protects their intent by ensuring that AI-assisted reasoning does not silently 
extend, reinterpret, or over-assert what those artifacts were designed to convey. 
Cognitive governance, as used here, is not a new domain of authority. It is a recognition that 
reasoning posture matters — and that preserving clarity at this level helps governance artifacts 
remain trustworthy and usable over time.

Access-Mode is intentionally modest.

Annex C — Author’s Intent (Informative) 
This paper was developed in response to a recurring pattern observed in AI-assisted 
governance work. As AI governance progresses, a wider range of tools, roles, and expectations 
is emerging. This often increases cognitive load, specialization pressure, and management 
overhead for those responsible for learning, operating, and reviewing governance materials. 
At the same time, AI systems are becoming more sophisticated and diverse in how they reason, 
explain, and analyze. When learning, operational analysis, and inspection reasoning are 
compressed into a single interaction, outputs may sound fluent while making it harder to see 
uncertainty, intent, or responsibility clearly. 
Access-Mode is presented as a method for slowing reasoning down on purpose, not to limit 
capability, but to make complex thinking easier to follow and easier to examine. By separating 
reasoning into clear postures and keeping those postures stable, the method helps people 
understand what kind of reasoning is taking place and what it can - and cannot - support. 
The intent of this work is to support governance practice in environments where complexity is 
increasing, so that AI assistance helps explain, organize, and clarify reasoning in ways that 
strengthen clarity, accountability, and human judgment. 
Why this matters: as AI becomes more capable and more widely used in governance contexts, 
the ability to clearly understand, question, and review reasoning becomes just as important as 
the conclusions that reasoning produces. 
Thank you for taking the time to read this paper.

istribution Statement 
This publication is released as a Public Review Draft (Standards Exploration). 
It may be used for: 
• academic research and comparative analysis,
• policy development and regulatory consultation,
• standards exploration and working-draft discussion, and
• evaluation of approaches to AI governance that move beyond static, documentation-based 
compliance toward engineered, runtime trust mechanisms.
• Feedback is invited to support refinement prior to subsequent editions and related 
artifacts.
This document does not constitute regulatory guidance, certification, or legal advice. It is intended to 
support informed review, discussion, and refinement of governance architectures, assurance models, 
and scoring methodologies for AI systems.

with emerging international AI standards.

Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) for pre-deployment and early-deployment risk discovery, a 
Policy-on-Demand (PoD) run-time governance engine for enforceable control execution, and a

architecture-specific extension using the Q-Pathformer system as a reference implementation.

1. Introduction 
Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed as long-lived, adaptive infrastructures rather 
than static software artifacts. As a result, governance approaches that rely primarily on documentation, 
one-time assessments, or post-hoc audits do not provide meaningful lifecycle assurance. This document 
introduces an operational governance framework designed to support continuous, evidence-based 
trust in AI systems as they evolve over time. 
1.1 The Limits of Static AI Compliance 
Traditional AI governance practices have emphasized static compliance mechanisms, including policy 
declarations, model cards, risk registers, and periodic audits. While such mechanisms may provide 
baseline accountability at a point in time, they do not provide lifecycle assurance for systems that: 
• are retrained, fine-tuned, or updated after deployment, 
• incorporate third-party models, tools, or data sources, 
• operate across heterogeneous environments and jurisdictions, or 
• exhibit emergent behavior through interaction with users and other systems. 
Static compliance frameworks shall not be considered sufficient to demonstrate ongoing conformity 
with safety, ethical, or regulatory expectations. In particular, they fail to capture runtime behavior, 
control degradation, and contextual misuse that may arise after initial approval. These gaps create a 
false sense of assurance and limit the ability of regulators, operators, and stakeholders to detect and 
respond to material risk. 
This document addresses these lifecycle assurance gaps by treating governance as an operational 
system, continuously evaluated through observable evidence rather than inferred intent. 
1.2 From Trust Declarations to Trust Engineering 
Many existing assurance approaches rely on attestation, whereby organizations declare that specified 
controls, principles, or processes are in place. Attestations assert intent or design, but they do not 
verify behavior. 
This document distinguishes clearly between: 
• Attestation-based assurance, which is document-centric and static; and 
• Telemetry-based assurance, which is evidence-centric and continuous.

Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP), the Access Policy-on-Demand (PoD) engine, and the Compliance 
Star Certificate (CSC) together implement this shift by embedding governance into system execution 
paths, rather than external reporting artifacts. 
1.3 Scope and Applicability Across AI & ML Systems 
This document specifies a governance and assurance layer that operates above AI system 
architectures, focusing on execution-time controls, telemetry, and evidence-based trust rather than 
model internals or training methodologies. 
The framework shall apply across a broad range of AI and ML system types, including: 
• classical machine learning pipelines; 
• computer vision systems; 
• deep learning architectures; 
• foundation models and large language models; and 
• agentic or tool-using AI systems.

structured_summary: Section: This section defines the conceptual foundations of the framework, establishing trust, transparency, and | Definitions: 1 | Rules: 5 | Constraints: 2 | Lifecycle logic: 1
excerpt:
This section defines the conceptual foundations of the framework, establishing trust, transparency, and 
responsibility as operational system properties. It further introduces a human-centric system maturity 
progression, first articulated in Volume 1, and refined in this second volume to support telemetry-driven 
governance and lifecycle assurance.

2.1 Trust, Transparency, and Responsibility in AI Systems 
For the purposes of this document, trust is defined as justified confidence that an AI system behaves 
within acceptable bounds under defined conditions and over time. Trust is not an intrinsic attribute of a 
model; it is an emergent property resulting from governance controls, system behavior, human 
oversight, and contextual constraints.

Transparency enables trust by making system behavior observable, explainable, and auditable. 
Transparency shall not be limited to static documentation or disclosures; it shall include runtime 
visibility into decision pathways, control enforcement, and system state.

Responsibility establishes accountability for outcomes. Responsibility shall be assignable, traceable, 
and enforceable across organizational, technical, and operational boundaries, including post-
deployment modification, reuse, and integration with external systems.

Together, trust, transparency, and responsibility form the minimum conceptual triad required for 
sustainable AI governance.

2.2 Human-Centric Governance as a System Property

Human-centric governance treats human judgment not as an external safeguard, but as an integrated 
system control. Human oversight shall be designed into workflows, escalation logic, and assurance 
mechanisms rather than applied retrospectively. 
Within this framework: 
• human intervention shall be available where risk exceeds predefined thresholds; 
• decisions shall be contestable through traceable evidence; and 
• escalation pathways shall be explicit, proportionate, and auditable. 
Human-centric governance therefore operates as a first-class system property, comparable to safety, 
security, or reliability controls, and not as an informal organizational practice.

2.3 System Maturity Progression (UIO-Defined Technologies)

Volume 1 introduced a human-centric maturity model for emerging technologies, describing how 
systems evolve from novelty to operational stability. This second volume refines that model by explicitly 
aligning each maturity stage with risk characteristics, governance needs, and assurance expectations.

Page | 8

The maturity progression consists of three stages: Under-defined, Informally defined, and Over-
defined.

2.3.1 Under-Defined Systems (Exploratory / High Uncertainty)

An under-defined system is one that is novel or emerging and may appear useful, compelling, or 
innovative, but whose behavior, boundaries, and impacts are not yet well understood. 
Such systems: 
• may sound, display, or express usefulness and interest; 
• often lack stable operating assumptions; 
• may introduce confusion, misuse, or unanticipated risk; and 
• exhibit high uncertainty regarding downstream impact. 
From a governance perspective, under-defined systems correspond to high uncertainty and 
unquantified risk exposure. Assurance at this stage shall focus on exploration, simulation, and risk 
discovery, rather than certification or deployment confidence. In this framework, Simulation AI-
Powered Policies (SAPP) are intended to operate primarily at this stage to surface latent risks before 
real-world impact occurs.

2.5 Alignment with International AI Standards 
The conceptual model defined in this section is designed to align with international standards while 
remaining implementation-agnostic: 
• ISO/IEC 42001: by treating governance as a management system with continuous improvement; 
• ISO/IEC 23894: by recognizing risk as dynamic and context-dependent; and 
• ISO/IEC 22989: by maintaining consistent terminology and system definitions. 
This document does not replace these standards. It provides an operational interpretation of their 
principles, suitable for evaluation through evidence rather than documentation alone.

3. Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) 
Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) provide the pre-deployment and early-deployment governance 
mechanism within the Access PoD framework. SAPP operationalizes governance by executing policies as 
code within controlled simulation environments, enabling risk discovery, control validation, and 
evidence generation prior to and during system deployment. 
SAPP is designed to support different governance objectives at different system maturity stages, as 
defined in Section 2.3. It therefore functions as a maturity-aware governance layer, rather than a one-
time assessment tool.

3.1 Purpose and Design Principles 
The primary purpose of SAPP is to surface, evaluate, and constrain risk before real-world impact 
occurs. SAPP shall enable organizations to test governance assumptions under realistic and adversarial 
conditions without exposing users, markets, or infrastructure to unvalidated behavior. 
SAPP is governed by the following design principles: 
• Simulation-first assurance: risk shall be explored through simulation before reliance on runtime 
controls. 
• Human-centric evaluation: simulation outcomes shall be interpretable and reviewable by 
human stakeholders. 
• Proportional governance: the depth of simulation shall scale with uncertainty and potential 
impact. 
• Evidence generation: simulation outputs shall produce machine-readable telemetry suitable for 
downstream assurance.

• enforce policy constraints prior to and after delegation; and

5. The Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) 
The Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) provides a continuous, telemetry-derived assurance mechanism 
for AI systems governed under the Access PoD framework. CSC shall not be interpreted as a static 
certification or compliance label. Instead, it functions as a dynamic trust signal derived from observable 
system behavior over time. 
CSC assurance is generated from evidence produced through Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) and 
runtime enforcement via the Access PoD engine. Certification shall reflect current governance 
performance, not historical approval.

5.1 From Compliance Artifacts to Continuous Assurance 
Traditional compliance approaches rely on artifacts such as policies, attestations, and audit reports. 
These artifacts describe intended controls, but they do not verify that controls remain effective during 
operation. 
CSC replaces artifact-based assurance with continuous evidence-based assurance. Within this 
framework: 
• certification shall be derived from telemetry, not documentation alone; 
• assurance shall degrade when evidence quality or control effectiveness degrades; and 
• governance shall be reassessed automatically as system behavior evolves. 
CSC shall not be issued in the absence of sufficient telemetry. Where evidence is incomplete or 
unavailable, CSC output shall be constrained, suspended, or withheld.

5.2 CSC Star Levels and ISO-Style Risk Tiers

approval. 
Star levels shall be mapped explicitly to ISO-aligned risk tiers, reflecting the extent to which identified

5.3 Certificate Lifecycle and Revocation Model 
CSC certification shall be continuous and lifecycle-aware. A CSC does not represent a point-in-time 
approval and shall not remain valid in the absence of supporting evidence. 
The CSC lifecycle shall include, at a minimum: 
• issuance based on sufficient telemetry; 
• continuous re-evaluation as new telemetry is generated; 
• downgrade where evidence indicates increased risk or control degradation; 
• suspension where evidence is incomplete or unreliable; and 
• revocation where critical governance failures are identified. 
Revocation shall not be treated as punitive. It is a protective control, indicating that trust claims are no 
longer supported by evidence. Re-issuance shall require renewed evidence, not administrative 
reinstatement.

5.4 Avoiding Certification-as-Status Ambiguity 
CSC shall not be treated as a status badge, marketing signal, or permanent designation. Any use of CSC 
output shall reflect its dynamic nature and be accompanied by current risk interpretation. 
Specifically: 
• CSC output shall not be cached or displayed without timestamp and validity context; 
• historical CSC levels shall not substitute for current assurance; and 
• changes in CSC level shall be considered material governance events.

6. CSC Scoring Rubric (Derived from SAPP Telemetry) 
The Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) scoring rubric defines the formal method by which governance 
performance is quantified using telemetry generated through Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) 
and runtime enforcement via the Access PoD engine. The rubric shall be evidence-driven, non-
compensatory, and continuously updateable, consistent with ISO/IEC risk management practices. 
CSC scores shall be computed, not assigned, and shall not exist independently of telemetry evidence.

6.1 Telemetry Domains and Evidence Sources 
CSC scoring shall be derived exclusively from telemetry evidence generated during simulation and 
runtime operation. Certification shall not rely on declarative compliance statements, documentation 
alone, or self-attestation. 
Telemetry evidence shall include, at a minimum: 
• SAPP simulation telemetry generated during pre-training and pre-deployment evaluation; 
• runtime-parity control telemetry captured during live system operation, where applicable; 
• human-in-the-loop interaction and intervention logs; and 
• policy-as-code execution traces and enforcement outcomes. 
Telemetry shall be structured, machine-readable, timestamped, and attributable to specific 
enforcement points and governance controls. Each telemetry domain shall map one-to-one with a

corresponding operational factor, ensuring that CSC scores reflect observed system behavior rather 
than inferred intent.

6.2 Factor-Level Scoring and Non-Compensatory Structure (Operational Factors 6.1–6.6)

CSC scoring is first calculated at the factor level, across six operational factors, each representing a 
distinct and essential governance domain: 
• 6.1 Industry 4.0 & Security 
• 6.2 Security & New Best Practice 
• 6.3 Best Practice & Compliance 
• 6.4 Compliance & Human-Centric Path 
• 6.5 Human-Centric & Trust-Transparency 
• 6.6 Trust-Transparency & Industry / Sector Alignment

Each factor shall be scored independently on a normalized 0–100 scale, based only on telemetry metrics 
relevant to that factor. No factor score is inferred from documentation or from performance in other 
domains.

6.5 Confidence, Drift, and Continuous Re-Scoring 
CSC certification shall be continuous and lifecycle-aware. Scores shall be recalculated as new telemetry 
is generated, enabling detection of system drift, control degradation, or changes in operational context. 
Re-scoring mechanisms shall account for: 
• telemetry completeness, freshness, and stability; 
• consistency of control enforcement over time; 
• effectiveness of human oversight mechanisms; and 
• deviation from previously validated behavioral baselines. 
Where telemetry confidence degrades or material drift is detected, CSC scores shall be downgraded, 
suspended, or revoked until corrective action is verified. This approach aligns CSC operation with 
ISO/IEC expectations for continuous risk monitoring and treatment, rather than point-in-time 
assessment.

7. Sector Anchoring and Industry Trust 
AI systems operate within distinct sectoral contexts, each characterized by different risk profiles, 
regulatory obligations, and societal expectations. Sector anchoring ensures that governance, assurance, 
and trust measurement remain context-aware, proportionate, and interpretable across domains. 
Within this framework, sector anchoring shall not alter the core CSC methodology. Instead, it refines 
how telemetry is weighted, interpreted, and governed, enabling comparability across sectors without 
imposing uniform risk assumptions.

7.1 Healthcare, Finance, and Public Sector Profiles 
Sector profiles align governance mechanisms with real-world impact, regulatory exposure, and 
domain-specific risk tolerance. Each sector profile shall define how CSC scoring is contextualized, 
without modifying the underlying factor structure. 
Sector-Specific Governance Characteristics 
• Healthcare 
Governance shall prioritize patient safety, clinical accountability, and explainability. Telemetry 
emphasis should include human-in-the-loop intervention, decision traceability, and outcome 
validation. Risk tolerance is low, and assurance degradation shall trigger immediate review. 
• Finance 
Governance shall emphasize security, fraud prevention, auditability, and systemic risk control. 
Telemetry should capture anomaly detection, control latency, and delegated decision 
accountability. Certification levels shall reflect exposure to market and consumer harm. 
• Public Sector 
Governance shall prioritize transparency, procedural fairness, contestability, and public 
accountability. Telemetry emphasis should include decision explainability, appeal handling, and 
policy adherence across jurisdictions.

7.2 Fair Competition, Credentialing, and Ecosystem Integrity 
CSC supports fair competition by making governance performance verifiable, comparable, and 
evidence-based, rather than reliant on claims, branding, or market dominance. 
Within this framework: 
• trust shall be earned through behavior, not asserted through reputation; 
• CSC scores shall be comparable across organizations operating in the same sector profile; and 
• assurance shall be portable, subject to scope and evidence validity.

The framework recognizes the role of first movers and exemplars in establishing early trust norms.

contributing patterns, tooling, and lessons learned to the broader ecosystem. 
Expertise sharing should be encouraged through: 
• publication of anonymized governance metrics; 
• contribution of reusable policy templates; and 
• shared learning from incident response and remediation. 
Such contributions shall not confer preferential certification status, but they may strengthen trust as a 
shared infrastructure by accelerating collective maturity.

Under traditional governance models, regulators primarily assess compliance through periodic audits, 
documentation reviews, and post-incident investigations. These approaches provide limited visibility 
into ongoing system behavior and are poorly suited to adaptive, continuously evolving AI systems.

Page | 24

Within this framework, regulators shall transition from audit-centric oversight to runtime evidence-
based supervision. 
Specifically, regulators shall be able to: 
• access continuous, machine-readable evidence derived from SAPP simulations and runtime 
telemetry; 
• interpret CSC outputs as current risk posture, not historical approval; 
• observe governance performance across system updates, scaling events, and cross-
organizational deployment; and 
• evaluate compliance drift as it occurs, rather than after harm has materialized.

Cross-Modal and Cross-Sector Visibility 
Runtime evidence may be exposed to regulators through controlled, role-appropriate interfaces that 
support: 
• cross-modal visibility (text, decision traces, control events, human review actions); 
• longitudinal views of organizational maturity and scaling behavior; and 
• sector-specific risk interpretation using declared sector profiles. 
This approach enables regulators to support development and scaling, not merely enforce constraints, 
by identifying early risk signals and governance gaps across industries and organizational stages.

This appendix specifies the formal method by which Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) telemetry 
is transformed into Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) scores through metric normalization, aggregation, 
and evidence verification. It defines procedures and structures required for evidence-based, continuous 
assurance, and does not introduce additional governance principles beyond those stated in the main 
body of this document.

A.1 Purpose of the CSC Scoring Rubric 
The Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) is a runtime-evidenced trust assurance mechanism, not a 
declarative or document-based compliance label. 
The CSC scoring rubric defines how CSC scores shall be computed directly from telemetry evidence, 
ensuring that: 
• certification reflects observed system behavior, not stated intent; 
• scores are continuously updateable as telemetry changes; 
• trust is earned, measurable, and revocable; and

Page | 31

• governance aligns with ISO-style risk management, rather than static assessment. 
CSC scores shall not be assigned manually. All scores shall be computed using the procedures defined 
in this appendix.

A.2 CSC Scoring Architecture (High Level) 
Inputs 
CSC computation shall consume the following telemetry inputs, where applicable: 
• SAPP simulation telemetry generated during pre-training and pre-deployment evaluation; 
• runtime-parity control telemetry captured during live system operation; 
• human-in-the-loop interaction and intervention logs; and 
• policy-as-code execution traces and enforcement outcomes.

Processing 
Telemetry inputs shall be processed through the following stages: 
1. Metric normalization 
2. Risk-weighted aggregation 
3. Factor-level scoring 
4. Star-level qualification gate evaluation 
Outputs 
CSC computation shall produce: 
• a CSC Star Rating (★–★★★★★★); 
• factor-level subscores corresponding to operational factors 6.1–6.6; 
• an ISO-aligned risk tier classification; and 
• a machine-readable evidence bundle supporting audit and verification.

A.3 Telemetry Domains 
CSC scoring draws from six telemetry domains, each mapped one-to-one with a corresponding 
operational factor. 
Each telemetry domain shall generate: 
• quantitative metrics, 
• qualitative signals, and 
• event traces. 
No factor score shall be computed where the corresponding telemetry domain is incomplete or 
unavailable.

A.4 Scoring Scale 
Each operational factor shall be scored on a normalized 0–100 scale, derived from weighted telemetry 
metrics associated with that factor. 
Scores shall be comparable across systems only within the same declared sector profile and scope.

A.5 Factor-Level Scoring Rubric 
A.5.1 Factor 6.1 — Industry 4.0 & Security (Trust) 
Telemetry sources include: 
• abuse and misuse simulation outcomes; 
• anomaly detection accuracy; 
• incident response latency; and 
• kill-switch and rollback activation success. 
Core metrics include: 
• percentage of simulated attacks detected; 
• mean time to containment (MTTC); 
• false positive and false negative rates; and 
• policy enforcement success rate.

Scoring logic: 
• <60: reactive security, weak containment 
• 60–79: active controls, inconsistent outcomes 
• 80–89: predictive detection, fast response 
• ≥90: proactive, low-latency, high-fidelity defense

A.5.2 Factor 6.2 — Security & New Best Practice (Trust) 
Telemetry sources include: 
• control adaptation frequency; 
• red-team and adversarial regression results; 
• supply-chain integrity checks; and 
• data-handling observability. 
Scoring logic: 
• <60: static security posture 
• 60–79: periodic updates, limited learning 
• 80–89: continuous hardening 
• ≥90: self-improving security posture

Executive Summary 
As artificial intelligence systems become adaptive, compositional, and continuously updated, 
governance approaches based on static documentation, point-in-time audits, and declarative 
compliance are no longer sufficient to sustain trust. 
Volume 2, Version A introduced a model-agnostic framework for engineering trust as a 
runtime system property, rather than treating it as an administrative outcome. That framework 
formalized three complementary mechanisms: 
1. Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) for pre-deployment and early-deployment risk 
discovery, 
2. a Policy-on-Demand (PoD) runtime governance engine for enforceable control 
execution, and 
3. a telemetry-derived Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) for continuous, revocable

CSC assurance is derived exclusively from observed system behavior, not documentation, 
intent, or attestation.

Purpose of Version B 
This Version B document introduces an architecture-specific extension using the Q-Pathformer 
system as a reference implementation. Its purpose is to demonstrate that the Version A 
governance framework can be operationalized at execution depth without embedding 
governance authority into system architecture. 
Version B shows: 
• how runtime governance controls can attach to real execution boundaries,

1. Introduction 
Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed as long-lived, adaptive infrastructures, 
rather than static software artifacts. As these systems evolve through retraining, fine-tuning, 
data augmentation, and integration with external services, governance approaches based on 
static documentation, point-in-time audits, or declarative compliance statements become 
insufficient to ensure sustained trust. 
Volume 2, Version A established a model-agnostic governance framework for AI systems based 
on three core mechanisms: 
• Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) for pre-deployment and early-deployment risk 
discovery, 
• a Policy-on-Demand (PoD) runtime governance engine for enforceable control 
execution, and 
• a telemetry-derived Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) for continuous, revocable 
assurance. 
That framework intentionally abstracted away from any specific AI architecture to ensure broad 
applicability across machine learning pipelines, foundation models, and agentic systems. 
This Version B document introduces an optional, architecture-specific extension, using the Q-
Pathformer system as a reference implementation. Its purpose is to demonstrate how the 
Version A governance framework may be instantiated at execution depth without altering, 
constraining, or redefining the core governance model. Within this framework, system 
onboarding is treated as a governed entry condition— establishing eligibility for controlled 
testing and evidence generation, rather than conferring trust, approval, or deployment 
readiness.

The objective of this chapter is to demonstrate how governance controls are executed,

3.1 Policy-as-Code Alignment 
Within the Version A framework, governance policies are defined as executable policy-as-code 
artifacts. These policies encode constraints, thresholds, and escalation conditions that are 
enforceable during system operation rather than relying on post-hoc review or documentation. 
In the context of this reference implementation: 
• Policy-as-code artifacts are evaluated and enforced by the Access PoD engine. 
• The reference architecture exposes explicit execution boundaries at which policies may 
be applied. 
• Policy evaluation outcomes are emitted as machine-readable telemetry for assurance 
purposes. 
Policy-as-code alignment does not require the architecture to implement governance logic 
internally. Instead, the architecture must expose sufficient interfaces and state signals to allow 
external policy execution to be effective. 
Governance policies shall therefore be architecture-aware but architecture-independent: 
aware of execution boundaries, yet not embedded within learning or inference logic.

4. UGCCMT Provenance Model 
This chapter introduces the UGCCMT provenance model as the architecture-specific 
mechanism used in this reference implementation to generate structured, machine-readable 
lineage and accountability signals for governance and assurance. 
UGCCMT— short for Unit–Group–Colour–Code–Measure–Train— is not a governance 
framework, scoring system, or certification mechanism. It is a provenance abstraction designed 
to ensure that governance-relevant activity within an AI system can be observed, attributed, 
and audited across the system lifecycle. 
Within Version B, UGCCMT is presented at the semantic and structural level only. 
Cryptographic sealing, validation, and enforcement mechanisms associated with UGCCMT are 
intentionally excluded from this public document and governed by restricted specifications.

4.1 Conceptual Overview of UGCCMT 
UGCCMT provides a structured method for describing how data, transformations, and learning 
events propagate through an AI system over time. 
At a conceptual level, UGCCMT defines six orthogonal dimensions: 
• Unit – the smallest addressable element subject to governance (e.g., a data element, 
token span, or interaction unit), 
• Group – a logical aggregation of units for lifecycle or governance purposes, 
• Colour – a categorical context or risk lens applied to the unit or group, 
• Code – the rule, constraint, or classification context under which processing occurs, 
• Measure – quantitative or qualitative signals generated through processing, and 
• Train – the lifecycle phase or learning context in which the unit participates. 
Together, these dimensions enable governance systems to answer fundamental questions such 
as: 
• What was processed? 
• Under what constraints? 
• In which lifecycle phase? 
• With what observed outcomes? 
UGCCMT does not dictate how learning occurs. It ensures that whatever occurs can be traced, 
contextualized, and reviewed.

4.3 Lineage, Traceability, and Audit Semantics 
UGCCMT is designed to support continuous lineage, rather than point-in-time traceability. 
Lineage within this model means that governance systems can reconstruct: 
• how a unit entered the system, 
• which transformations or training phases it participated in, 
• which policy constraints were applicable at each stage, and 
• which measurable outcomes were observed. 
UGCCMT records are generated as an inherent output of execution, not as an after-the-fact 
annotation process. This ensures that provenance reflects actual system behavior rather than 
reconstructed intent.

4.3 Lineage, Traceability, and Audit Semantics 
UGCCMT is designed to support continuous lineage, rather than point-in-time traceability. 
Lineage within this model means that governance systems can reconstruct: 
• how a unit entered the system, 
• which transformations or training phases it participated in, 
• which policy constraints were applicable at each stage, and 
• which measurable outcomes were observed. 
UGCCMT records are generated as an inherent output of execution, not as an after-the-fact 
annotation process. This ensures that provenance reflects actual system behavior rather than 
reconstructed intent.

Page | 21

UGCCMT does not itself perform audits, assign trust scores, or issue assurance claims. Instead, 
it provides the semantic substrate upon which: 
• Access PoD enforces runtime governance, 
• SAPP evaluates risk through simulation, and 
• CSC derives evidence-based assurance signals. 
Cryptographic sealing, validation, and tamper-resistance mechanisms that protect UGCCMT 
records are specified separately in restricted documentation and are intentionally out of scope 
for Version B.

Normative Summary (Chapter 4) 
• UGCCMT defines a provenance and lineage abstraction, not a governance framework. 
• The model is modality-agnostic and lifecycle-aware. 
• UGCCMT records enable attribution, traceability, and audit across execution phases. 
• UGCCMT does not prescribe learning behavior or performance characteristics. 
• Cryptographic realization and enforcement of UGCCMT records are out of scope for this 
document.

5. API Governance and Controlled Execution Interfaces 
This chapter defines the governance principles, control boundaries, and execution constraints 
applicable to application programming interfaces (APIs) used for data procurement, training 
execution, and model lifecycle operations within the reference implementation. 
APIs are treated within this framework not as neutral transport mechanisms, but as 
governance-critical execution boundaries. Their design, scope, and authorization model 
directly affect the integrity, traceability, and safety of governed AI systems.

5.1 Governance–Execution Separation 
A fundamental requirement of this framework is the explicit separation of governance 
authority from execution capability. 
Accordingly: 
• Access PoD shall serve as the governance, proposal, evaluation, and authorization layer. 
• Execution APIs, including the Q-Pathformer API, shall operate solely as controlled 
execution interfaces. 
No API endpoint shall be permitted to simultaneously: 
1. propose new datasets, training objectives, or configuration changes; 
2. approve such proposals; and 
3. execute training, ingestion, or artifact modification. 
This separation is a mandatory safeguard against uncontrolled system evolution and prevents 
governance bypass through API misuse or misconfiguration.

5.2 APIs as Policy-Bound Execution Nodes 
Each governed API interface shall be treated as a policy-bound execution node. 
An execution node is defined as an interface that: 
• receives requests only through authenticated and authorized governance pathways, 
• enforces declared scope, purpose, and lifecycle constraints prior to execution, and 
• emits machine-readable telemetry as a first-class output.

Page | 23

Execution nodes shall not operate as general-purpose ingress points. Instead, they shall be 
explicitly scoped to: 
• approved datasets and dataset versions, 
• approved training or execution objectives, 
• approved lifecycle stages (e.g., evaluation, training, promotion), and 
• approved assurance contexts. 
This node-based design limits the blast radius of execution-level failures and supports fine-
grained attribution and audit.

All proposals for: 
• new data procurement, 
• dataset updates or extensions, 
• retraining, fine-tuning, or harmonization events, and 
• material configuration or lifecycle changes, 
shall originate within the Access PoD governance workflow. 
Such proposals shall: 
• be evaluated against applicable policy constraints and sector profiles, 
• be subjected to Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) where required, and 
• require explicit authorization prior to execution. 
Execution APIs, including the Q-Pathformer API, shall not independently source, approve, or 
prioritize training data. 
This constraint ensures that data governance remains upstream of execution and that 
provenance integrity is preserved across the system lifecycle.

serves as the exclusive controlled execution interface for approved training and dataset

5.5 Third-Party Model APIs and Standards Participation 
Third-party model APIs may participate in the Access PoD ecosystem subject to standards-
mediated confirmation. 
Participation conditions shall include: 
• explicit declaration of execution scope and intended use, 
• compatibility with Access PoD governance signals and telemetry requirements, and 
• confirmation by relevant standards bodies, sector authorities, or governance councils 
where applicable. 
Third-party APIs shall not bypass Access PoD controls. Where external models are invoked, 
governance responsibility and assurance obligations shall remain with the integrating 
organization. 
This model enables interoperability while preserving accountability and preventing ungoverned 
execution paths.

5.6 Catastrophic Overwrite Prevention 
Within this framework, catastrophic overwrite— defined as uncontrolled, irreversible 
modification of governed datasets, model artifacts, or lineage records— is treated as a systemic 
security risk.

Page | 25

Accordingly: 
• execution APIs shall enforce controlled versioning or immutability where applicable, 
• overwriting of governed artifacts shall require explicit governance authorization, and 
• rollback, revocation, and lineage continuity shall be supported as protective controls. 
Catastrophic overwrite prevention is a governance security objective, not a performance 
optimization or implementation detail. It is essential for maintaining trust, auditability, and 
long-term system integrity. This constraint applies equally during testing, evaluation, and 
governance stress scenarios.

6. Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) Integration 
This chapter defines how the Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) is integrated with the reference 
architecture to provide continuous, telemetry-derived assurance. CSC integration in Version B 
demonstrates how execution-level telemetry and provenance signals are transformed into 
interpretable trust indicators, while preserving the authority, semantics, and scoring logic 
defined in Version A. 
CSC is not a static certification, endorsement, or approval. It is a dynamic assurance signal 
derived exclusively from observed system behavior.

6.1 CSC Evidence Inputs from Architecture Telemetry 
CSC evidence shall be derived exclusively from telemetry generated during simulation and 
runtime operation, in accordance with Version A requirements. 
Within the reference implementation, CSC evidence inputs include: 
• governance enforcement telemetry emitted by Access PoD at defined execution 
boundaries, 
• SAPP simulation outputs associated with proposed changes or elevated-risk scenarios, 
• UGCCMT provenance and lineage records describing lifecycle participation and context, 
and 
• human-in-the-loop intervention and escalation events. 
The architecture’s role is limited to producing accurate, attributable telemetry. It does not 
compute CSC scores, assign star levels, or interpret assurance outcomes. 
Where telemetry is incomplete, delayed, or unavailable, CSC computation shall be constrained, 
suspended, or withheld, consistent with Version A non-compensatory scoring principles.

6.2 Assurance Boundaries and Interpretation 
CSC integration preserves a strict separation between evidence production and assurance 
interpretation. 
Accordingly: 
• CSC scores are computed by governance mechanisms external to the architecture.

6.2 Assurance Boundaries and Interpretation 
CSC integration preserves a strict separation between evidence production and assurance 
interpretation. 
Accordingly: 
• CSC scores are computed by governance mechanisms external to the architecture.

Page | 27

• CSC star levels represent current risk posture and governance maturity, not quality, 
performance, or suitability. 
• CSC outputs shall be interpreted only within their declared scope, sector profile, and 
validity context. 
No CSC output shall be cached, reused, or displayed without: 
• a timestamp, 
• a scope declaration, and 
• an indication of evidence freshness. 
Architecture-specific behavior shall not modify CSC semantics. A change in execution behavior 
affects CSC only through changes in observed telemetry, not through architectural designation 
or status. CSC shall therefore be interpreted strictly as a transient governance signal, not as 
a certiﬁcation, endorsement, or standing designation. 
6.3 Revocation and Degradation Semantics 
CSC integration in Version B explicitly supports assurance degradation and revocation as first-
class governance outcomes. 
CSC degradation or revocation may occur when: 
• governance controls fail to enforce policy at defined execution boundaries, 
• telemetry confidence degrades or becomes incomplete, 
• material drift is detected between simulated and observed behavior, or 
• human-centric oversight requirements are not met. 
Revocation is a protective control, not a punitive action. It signals that trust claims are no 
longer supported by evidence and that corrective action or re-evaluation is required prior to 
reinstatement. 
Re-issuance of CSC assurance shall require renewed evidence generation and evaluation. 
Administrative reinstatement without supporting telemetry shall not be permitted.

6.4 Evidence Packaging and Proportional Disclosure (Informative) 
While CSC assurance is computed as a continuous signal, Version B recognizes that regulatory 
and audit interactions frequently require evidence packaging rather than raw telemetry access.

6.4 Evidence Packaging and Proportional Disclosure (Informative) 
While CSC assurance is computed as a continuous signal, Version B recognizes that regulatory 
and audit interactions frequently require evidence packaging rather than raw telemetry access.

Page | 28

For this purpose, CSC-relevant signals may be aggregated into governed evidence bundles 
representing increasing sensitivity and disclosure depth. These bundles are intended to support 
proportional oversight by enabling: 
• confirmation of evidence existence and integrity, 
• controlled, time-bound access aligned to authority level, and 
• selective disclosure based on necessity rather than convenience. 
Importantly, evidence packaging does not alter CSC semantics, scoring logic, or authority. It is 
an assurance-delivery construct that operates downstream of CSC computation and remains 
subordinate to the governance framework defined in Version A.

• CSC assurance shall be derived exclusively from telemetry evidence. 
• Architecture supplies evidence; governance computes and interprets assurance. 
• CSC star levels represent risk posture, not approval or performance. 
• Assurance shall be scope-bound, time-bound, and revocable. 
• Degradation and revocation are expected governance outcomes when evidence 
degrades.

7. Security, Trust, and Responsibility Boundaries 
This section defines the security, trust, and responsibility boundaries applicable to the 
architecture-specific extension introduced in Version B. It clarifies what aspects of system 
behavior are governed, what aspects are explicitly excluded, and how responsibility is 
preserved across governance, execution, and assurance layers. 
These boundaries are essential to prevent misinterpretation of Version B as a security 
specification, operational manual, or certification regime.

7.1 What Is Governed in Version B 
Version B governs how governance controls are instantiated at execution boundaries, not how 
AI systems are internally designed, optimized, or deployed. 
Specifically, Version B governs: 
• Governance execution boundaries, including where and how policies are enforced at 
runtime via Access PoD; 
• Telemetry generation and attribution, ensuring governance-relevant behavior is 
observable, timestamped, and attributable; 
• Provenance and lineage semantics, via the UGCCMT model, sufficient to support audit, 
traceability, and lifecycle reasoning; 
• Controlled execution interfaces, including API-level safeguards against ungoverned data 
ingestion or artifact modification; and 
• Assurance interpretation boundaries, ensuring CSC outputs remain evidence-derived, 
scope-bound, time-bound, and revocable. 
Governance in Version B is concerned with control effectiveness and evidence integrity, not 
internal learning correctness, model quality, or system performance.

Version B: 
• cryptographic algorithms, parameters, key management, or signature schemes; 
• validation node internals, trust models, or quorum assumptions; 
• security thresholds, drift metrics, re-derivation triggers, or incident response playbooks; 
• training algorithms, optimization strategies, or model-internal mechanics;

9. Conclusion 
This document has presented an architecture-specific extension to the Volume 2 governance 
framework defined in Version A, using the Q-Pathformer system as a reference 
implementation. 
The extension demonstrates that: 
• runtime governance controls can be instantiated at execution depth without embedding 
governance authority in system architecture, 
• continuous, telemetry-derived assurance is feasible for adaptive AI systems, and 
• trust can be engineered, observed, degraded, and revoked based on evidence rather 
than declaration. 
Version B preserves the architecture-agnostic integrity of the original framework while 
providing concrete grounding for reviewers, policymakers, and system designers seeking to 
evaluate governance feasibility beyond abstraction.

9.1 Engineering Trust Before Impact 
Trust in AI systems shall not be inferred from documentation, intent, or reputation. It must be 
engineered before impact occurs and sustained through continuous observation and control. 
By integrating: 
• simulation-first risk discovery (SAPP), 
• runtime policy enforcement (Access PoD), and 
• evidence-based assurance (CSC), 
this framework enables governance to operate proactively rather than reactively, reducing 
systemic risk while supporting responsible innovation.

9.2 Standards, Conformance, and Ongoing Evolution 
This document does not claim to define a final or exclusive standard. 
Instead, it provides a reference architecture extension through which governance practices 
may be tested, compared, and refined. Standards leadership is expected to emerge from 
validated, repeatable practice, not assertion.

• Governs disclosure by authority, time, and necessity. 
• Enables third-party confirmation without content exposure. 
Each layer is independently observable and mutually constraining, enabling validation of 
intent, direction, and operational validity.

How This Framework Differs from Certification Schemes 
(Informative — Clarifying Note for Regulators) 
This document and its associated mechanisms are not a certification scheme and should not be 
interpreted as such. 
The framework described in this volume differs from traditional certification models in several 
fundamental ways. 
1. Certification vs. Continuous Assurance 
Traditional certification schemes: 
• assess systems at a point in time, 
• rely on documentation, attestations, and audits, and 
• issue a status that remains valid until expiry or revocation through external action. 
By contrast, this framework: 
• derives assurance continuously from observed system behavior, 
• treats trust as time-bound and evidence-dependent, and 
• supports automatic degradation or revocation when evidence no longer supports prior 
trust claims. 
If telemetry does not exist, assurance does not exist.

2. Status Labels vs. Evidence-Derived Signals 
Certification schemes typically issue: 
• binary or tiered status labels (certified / not certified), 
• often reused across contexts and deployments. 
The Compliance Star Certificate (CSC): 
• is a computed assurance signal, not a designation,

Page | 51

• is explicitly scope-bound, time-stamped, and contextual, and 
• cannot be reused, transferred, or cached without fresh evidence. 
CSC star levels represent current governance risk posture, not approval, quality, or fitness for 
purpose.

3. Approval Authority vs. Governance Infrastructure 
Certification schemes typically: 
• assert approval authority, and 
• function as gatekeepers for market access or compliance claims. 
This framework: 
• does not approve systems, 
• does not confer regulatory status, and 
• does not replace sector-specific compliance regimes. 
It provides governance infrastructure that regulators may observe, interrogate, or integrate 
with existing oversight mechanisms.

This briefing is provided to assist regulators, standards bodies, and public-sector oversight

1. Problem Statement: Limits of Existing AI Oversight Models 
Current AI oversight mechanisms rely heavily on: 
• documentation and attestations, 
• point-in-time audits, 
• static risk registers, and 
• post-incident investigations. 
These mechanisms are poorly suited to modern AI systems that are: 
• continuously retrained or updated, 
• composed of multiple models and external services, 
• deployed across jurisdictions and organizational boundaries, and 
• capable of emergent behavior over time. 
As a result, regulators face a visibility gap between what systems are declared to do and how 
they actually behave during operation.

2. Core Regulatory Shift Introduced by This Framework 
This framework proposes a shift from compliance as declaration to assurance as evidence. 
Rather than asking:

Page | 54

“Does the system claim to meet requirements?” 
the framework enables regulators to ask: 
“What does the system demonstrably do, under real conditions, over time?” 
This is achieved through three integrated mechanisms: 
1. Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) — pre-deployment and early-deployment risk 
discovery, 
2. Access Policy-on-Demand (PoD) — runtime enforcement and telemetry generation, and 
3. Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) — continuous, revocable assurance derived from 
evidence.

3. What Regulators Can Observe (and What They Do Not Need to Trust) 
Under this model, regulators are not asked to trust: 
• internal model architecture, 
• proprietary training techniques, 
• cryptographic implementation detail, or 
• vendor claims of “responsible AI.” 
Instead, regulators can observe: 
• runtime governance telemetry, including policy enforcement outcomes, 
• simulation evidence showing how systems behave under stress or misuse, 
• human-in-the-loop intervention records, and 
• assurance degradation or revocation events when controls fail. 
If telemetry does not exist, assurance does not exist.

4. Compliance Star Certificate (CSC): What It Is and What It Is Not 
What CSC Is 
• A dynamic assurance signal, not a certification. 
• Computed continuously from runtime and simulation telemetry. 
• Explicitly scope-bound, time-bound, and revocable. 
• Aligned with ISO/IEC risk-management principles.

Page | 55

CSC star levels represent current governance risk posture, not system quality, performance, or 
approval. 
What CSC Is Not 
• Not a regulatory certification. 
• Not a compliance label. 
• Not a one-time approval. 
• Not transferable without scope and evidence review. 
This avoids the common regulatory pitfall of certification-as-status.

5. Architecture-Specific Reference (Version B Context) 
Version B introduces a reference implementation using the Q-Pathformer system to 
demonstrate feasibility at execution depth. 
This reference implementation is used solely to show: 
• how governance attaches to execution boundaries, 
• how telemetry is generated from real system behavior, and 
• how catastrophic data or model overwrite can be prevented through API-level 
governance. 
Importantly: 
• Governance authority does not reside in the architecture. 
• Regulators are not required to endorse or adopt the reference system. 
• The governance framework remains architecture-agnostic.

6. Regulatory Advantages of This Approach 
For regulators, this model provides: 
• Continuous oversight, not episodic audits. 
• Early warning signals through simulation and telemetry. 
• Evidence-based enforcement, not documentation disputes. 
• Clear revocation semantics when trust degrades. 
• Interoperability, allowing oversight across vendors and sectors.

Page | 56

This approach is compatible with: 
• EU AI Act lifecycle risk management, 
• ISO/IEC 42001 AI management systems, 
• sector-specific safety and accountability regimes.

7. What This Framework Does Not Do 
This framework does not: 
• replace sector-specific regulation, 
• define legal compliance thresholds, 
• mandate specific technical architectures, 
• expose sensitive security or cryptographic mechanisms, or 
• shift responsibility away from system operators. 
It provides governance infrastructure, not regulatory authority.

8. Key Takeaway for Regulators 
This framework enables regulators to move from: 
“Trust us — we comply.” 
to: 
“Here is what the system actually did, when, under which controls, and with what outcome.” 
Trust becomes observable, measurable, and revocable.

Executive Summary — Version C 
Onboarding & Operational Transition for Runtime AI Governance 
Volume 2 — Version C addresses a critical and often under-specified phase in AI governance: 
onboarding into runtime operation. While Version A defines the authoritative framework for 
evidence-based, runtime AI governance, and Version B demonstrates feasibility at execution 
depth, neither specifies how organizations should enter governance responsibly without 
asserting trust prematurely. 
Version C fills this gap. 
Purpose and positioning 
Version C is a transitional, operational guidance document. It does not introduce new 
governance principles, assurance semantics, or scoring logic. Instead, it clarifies how 
organizations, regulators, and standards bodies should interpret and manage the transition 
from design-time intent to runtime governance, particularly under conditions of uncertainty. 
Version C is explicitly subordinate to Version A and complementary to Version B. Where 
ambiguity arises, Version A remains authoritative.

Core insight: containment precedes alignment 
Version C is grounded in a clear distinction: 
• Containment is an operational requirement: the ability to govern AI systems while they 
are running through runtime controls, evidence generation, escalation, and revocation. 
• Alignment is a governance maturity outcome that strengthens over time as 
containment capability, tooling, standards, and professional expertise evolve. 
Version C treats containment as a prerequisite, not a consequence, of alignment. Alignment 
cannot be reliably assumed at onboarding and must not be asserted in the absence of 
operational containment.

Relationship to Q-Pathformer 
Q-Pathformer is treated strictly as an optional, non-normative reference substrate that may be 
used during onboarding to exercise and inspect runtime governance mechanisms under 
controlled conditions. Governance authority, assurance interpretation, and trust signals remain 
external and independent of any execution substrate. 
Organizations are expected to transition beyond reference implementations as governance 
capability matures, without redefining governance principles.

Page | 4

Why this matters 
Onboarding is the most fragile phase of AI system operation. It is where governance failure is 
most likely to be masked by documentation, optimism, or reputational assumptions. 
By formalizing onboarding as a governed transition: 
• false confidence is reduced; 
• certification-by-association is avoided; 
• regulators gain clearer visibility into early governance behavior; and 
• alignment is allowed to mature safely under containment.

Outcome 
Version C makes the Volume 2 framework operable in practice without weakening its 
standards credibility. It provides a disciplined pathway into runtime governance, after which 
continuous assurance, revocation semantics, and interoperability remain governed exclusively 
by Version A. 
Trust is not granted at entry. 
It is engineered, observed, and maintained— continuously.

1. Purpose and Scope of Version C 
Volume 2 — Version C defines the onboarding and operational transition context for the 
governance framework specified in Version A and instantiated illustratively in Version B. Its 
purpose is to clarify how organizations may enter runtime AI governance in a controlled, 
evidence-based manner, without treating onboarding as approval, certification, or deployment 
endorsement. 
Version C does not introduce new governance principles, assurance semantics, or scoring logic. 
Instead, it provides a governed transition reference that preserves the separation between 
governance authority, system execution, and assurance interpretation established in earlier 
editions. 
This section explains why onboarding itself must be treated as a governed activity, what 
Version C is intended to enable, and who the document is written for.

1.1 Why onboarding requires governance discipline 
Onboarding an AI system into operation is a high-risk transition point in the system lifecycle. It 
is the moment at which theoretical governance intent meets real execution behavior, often 
under incomplete knowledge of downstream impact, emergent behavior, or integration effects. 
In many contemporary AI deployments, onboarding is treated as an administrative milestone—
characterized by documentation reviews, sign-offs, or policy acknowledgements. Such 
approaches implicitly assume that governance maturity exists at the point of entry. In practice, 
this assumption is frequently invalid. 
From the perspective of this framework: 
• onboarding precedes alignment maturity; 
• operational behavior is not yet fully understood; and 
• risk profiles are provisional and subject to change. 
Without governance discipline at onboarding, organizations may inadvertently: 
• assert trust before evidence exists, 
• conflate readiness with compliance, 
• or allow systems to operate without effective containment mechanisms.

Version C therefore treats onboarding not as an approval event, but as a governed entry 
condition— one in which containment, evidence generation, escalation, and revocation 
mechanisms must be demonstrably in place before trust can begin to be earned.

1.2 What Version C enables (and what it explicitly does not) 
Version C enables reviewers and operators to understand how runtime governance is entered 
responsibly, while maintaining strict scope discipline. 
Specifically, Version C enables: 
• a shared understanding of onboarding phases aligned to system maturity; 
• clarity on when Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP), the Access Policy-on-Demand 
(PoD) engine, and Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) mechanisms may be activated; 
• explicit articulation of authority boundaries during early operation; 
• alignment between organizational roles, governance controls, and evidence 
expectations; and 
• regulator- and standards-facing review of transition discipline. 
Version C explicitly does not: 
• imply trust, readiness, or regulatory determination; 
• define deployment readiness or fitness for purpose; 
• prescribe technical implementations, APIs, or configurations; 
• modify governance principles, CSC semantics, or scoring logic defined in Version A; or 
• elevate any reference architecture, including Q-Pathformer, to a normative 
requirement. 
By design, Version C avoids implementation prescription. Its function is to constrain unsafe 
inference and misuse by defining what onboarding means in governance terms, not how 
systems must be built. 
Policy Evolution Boundary (Clarification) 
Version C recognizes that AI systems may operate within environments where legacy policies, 
proposed policy instruments, and amended or evolving policy frameworks coexist. Such 
conditions are common during regulatory transition, standards development, and early system 
deployment. 
However, Version C does not define, prescribe, or formalize how policies are drafted, amended, 
ratified, or superseded. The establishment, amendment, or withdrawal of policy authority

2. Containment and Alignment in the Context of Onboarding 
This section clarifies the distinct but related roles of containment and alignment during the 
onboarding phase of AI system operation. It establishes why containment must be treated as an 
operational prerequisite, while alignment is understood as a governance maturity outcome 
that strengthens over time. 
Within the Volume 2 framework, onboarding is not the point at which alignment can be 
reasonably assumed. It is the point at which containment must be demonstrably established so 
that alignment may evolve safely, measurably, and under continuous oversight.

2.1 Containment as an operational requirement 
Containment, within the context of this framework, refers to the operational ability to govern 
an AI system while it is running. It is concerned with whether governance controls are 
executable, observable, and enforceable under real operating conditions. 
Containment is not a theoretical construct. It is defined by the presence of concrete 
mechanisms that constrain behavior, generate evidence, and enable proportionate intervention 
when conditions change. 
At onboarding, containment is required because system behavior, interaction patterns, and risk 
exposure are not yet fully characterized. Governance must therefore be capable of responding 
to uncertainty rather than presuming stability. 
Operational containment consists, at a minimum, of the following elements. 
Runtime controls 
Runtime controls define where and how governance is enforced during system execution. 
These controls operate at identified enforcement points, such as decision gateways, data access 
interfaces, delegation boundaries, and lifecycle transition events. 
Runtime controls ensure that: 
• governance constraints are applied concurrently with execution; 
• policy violations can be detected as they occur; and 
• control failures are observable rather than inferred after the fact. 
Without runtime controls, governance remains external to system behavior and cannot 
function as an operational safeguard.

At onboarding, evidence generation establishes the baseline from which governance maturity

Escalation and revocation 
Containment must include explicit escalation pathways and revocation mechanisms. These 
mechanisms ensure that governance responses scale with risk and that trust is not treated as 
irrevocable. 
Escalation mechanisms: 
• route elevated-risk events to appropriate human oversight; 
• support contestability and review; and 
• preserve accountability across organizational boundaries. 
Revocation mechanisms: 
• enable suspension or degradation of trust signals when evidence degrades; 
• prevent continued operation under invalid assumptions; and 
• function as protective controls rather than punitive actions. 
Together, escalation and revocation distinguish containment from passive monitoring.

2.2 Alignment as a governance maturity outcome 
Alignment refers to the degree to which an AI system’s behavior consistently reflects human, 
legal, and societal intent across contexts and over time. Within this framework, alignment is 
not treated as a binary property or a precondition for onboarding. 
Alignment strengthens as governance capability matures. It improves through:

Page | 14

• repeated exposure to real operational conditions; 
• refinement of policies and controls; 
• accumulation of high-quality evidence; and 
• development of specialized expertise across policy, engineering, risk, and oversight 
roles. 
Because alignment depends on observed behavior and institutional learning, it cannot be 
reliably asserted at the point of onboarding. 
Why alignment strengthens over time 
As systems move from under-defined to informally defined and eventually over-defined 
maturity stages, governance mechanisms become more effective at: 
• detecting drift and misuse; 
• adapting controls to emerging patterns; and 
• stabilizing expectations around acceptable behavior. 
Alignment, in this sense, is an outcome of sustained containment and governance practice, not 
a prerequisite that can be certified in advance. 
Why alignment cannot be assumed at onboarding 
At onboarding, uncertainty is inherent. Claims of alignment at this stage are necessarily 
provisional and risk creating false confidence if not supported by operational evidence. 
Assuming alignment prematurely may: 
• mask latent risks; 
• discourage scrutiny and adaptation; and 
• undermine trust when deviations inevitably occur. 
Version C therefore treats alignment as something to be governed toward, not something to 
be declared at entry.

Containment must precede alignment because it provides the conditions under which 
alignment can be evaluated meaningfully.

Alignment claims made in the absence of operational containment represent a systemic 
governance failure mode. 
Such claims often rely on: 
• design-time intent; 
• policy declarations; or 
• static assessments disconnected from runtime behavior.

• cannot be verified continuously; 
• cannot respond proportionately to change; and 
• cannot support revocation when assumptions fail.

conferred by intent, reputation, or stated values. It is earned and maintained through 
containment mechanisms that make alignment observable, contestable, and revisable over 
time.

3. Governance Maturity and Onboarding Phases 
This section describes how AI systems enter and progress through runtime governance in 
accordance with the human-centric system maturity model introduced in Volume 1 and

The maturity stages— under-defined, informally defined, and over-defined— are not abstract

Progression between phases shall be supported by observable evidence, not by declaration,

3.1 Under-defined systems: exploratory onboarding 
An under-defined system is one whose behavior, boundaries, and downstream impacts are not 
yet well understood. At onboarding, such systems often appear promising or innovative but 
exhibit high uncertainty and unquantified risk. 
Exploratory onboarding for under-defined systems shall prioritize containment and learning, 
not confidence or approval. 
At this phase: 
• system behavior is treated as provisional; 
• assumptions are explicitly testable; and 
• deployment confidence is intentionally constrained. 
Governance at this stage shall emphasize: 
• simulation-first evaluation through SAPP; 
• limited operational exposure; 
• strict enforcement of escalation pathways; and 
• prohibition of static assurance claims. 
No continuous assurance signal shall be issued for under-defined systems beyond exploratory 
or internal analysis. Onboarding at this stage establishes eligibility for observation, not trust.

evidence is produced.

5. Technical Onboarding (Non-Prescriptive) 
This section defines the technical readiness conditions required to support governed 
onboarding into runtime AI governance. It does not prescribe system architectures, interfaces, 
or implementation details. Instead, it specifies what must be observable and controllable 
before governance mechanisms may be relied upon. 
Technical onboarding, within Version C, is concerned with governability, not optimization. A 
system that cannot be observed, constrained, or evidenced at runtime cannot be governed, 
regardless of performance or design intent.

5.1 Identifying execution boundaries 
Execution boundaries are the points at which system behavior may produce material impact 
and therefore require governance oversight. Identifying these boundaries is a prerequisite for 
operational containment. 
Execution boundaries may include, but are not limited to: 
• decision or inference gateways; 
• data access, transformation, or output interfaces; 
• delegation to external models, tools, or services; 
• lifecycle transitions such as retraining, fine-tuning, or configuration change; and 
• human interaction points with potential downstream effect. 
At onboarding, organizations shall be able to identify and enumerate execution boundaries 
relevant to the system’s current maturity stage. Where boundaries cannot be identified, 
governance enforcement cannot be meaningfully applied.

5.2 Declaring enforcement points 
Enforcement points are execution boundaries at which governance controls may be applied. 
Declaring enforcement points does not require implementation detail, but it does require 
clarity of intent and scope. 
For onboarding purposes: 
• enforcement points shall be explicitly declared; 
• each enforcement point shall be attributable to a governance context; and 
• enforcement points shall support observable outcomes (e.g., allow, block, escalate).

Page | 25

Enforcement points establish where governance authority may act. Without declared 
enforcement points, containment remains theoretical and cannot be exercised under real 
conditions.

5.3 Telemetry readiness checks 
Telemetry readiness refers to the system’s ability to produce governance-relevant signals 
during operation. Telemetry is required to support evidence-based assurance and lifecycle 
evaluation. 
At onboarding, telemetry readiness shall be assessed by confirming that: 
• governance-relevant events are observable; 
• telemetry is attributable to defined enforcement points; 
• signals are timestamped and contextualized; and 
• telemetry generation is continuous rather than episodic. 
Telemetry readiness does not require that all metrics be finalized or optimized. It requires only 
that sufficient signals exist to support containment, review, and escalation. Where telemetry 
is absent or unreliable, assurance claims shall not be made.

5.4 Evidence continuity requirements 
Evidence continuity ensures that governance-relevant evidence remains coherent across 
system lifecycle events, including updates, retraining, delegation, and scaling. 
For onboarding: 
• evidence shall persist across execution sessions; 
• changes to system state shall not invalidate prior evidence without traceability; 
• evidence gaps shall be detectable; and 
• loss of evidence continuity shall be treated as a governance event. 
Evidence continuity is necessary to prevent false confidence arising from partial visibility or 
selective observation. Where evidence continuity cannot be maintained, trust signals shall be 
constrained or withheld.

6. Access PoD in the Onboarding Lifecycle 
This section describes how the Access Policy-on-Demand (PoD) framework operates during 
onboarding to support containment, evidence generation, and controlled transition into 
runtime governance. It clarifies the role of Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP), runtime 
policy activation, and early-phase escalation, while explicitly constraining what onboarding 
does not imply. 
Access PoD does not confer trust at onboarding. It enables governed exposure, allowing 
organizations to observe behavior, test assumptions, and intervene proportionately as evidence 
accumulates.

6.1 SAPP at onboarding (simulation-first containment) 
Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP) provide the primary containment mechanism at 
onboarding, particularly for under-defined and informally defined systems. 
At onboarding, SAPP shall be used to: 
• evaluate proposed execution paths under simulated conditions; 
• explore misuse, edge cases, and adversarial scenarios; 
• test governance assumptions prior to runtime reliance; and 
• generate preliminary evidence to inform whether and how operation may proceed. 
Simulation-first containment ensures that novelty, apparent usefulness, or deployment 
pressure do not bypass governance validation. SAPP outputs at this stage are informative, not 
certifying. They support learning, constraint refinement, and human review before confidence 
is asserted. 
Where simulation outcomes indicate elevated or poorly understood risk, onboarding shall 
remain constrained until further evidence is produced.

6.2 Runtime policy activation 
Runtime policy activation marks the transition from simulation-only governance to concurrent 
governance during execution. This activation shall occur only after minimum onboarding 
conditions defined in Section 5 are met.

structured_summary: Section: 6.2 Runtime policy activation | Rules: 3 | Constraints: 4 | Lifecycle logic: 7 | Naming/IDs: 1
excerpt:
6.2 Runtime policy activation 
Runtime policy activation marks the transition from simulation-only governance to concurrent 
governance during execution. This activation shall occur only after minimum onboarding 
conditions defined in Section 5 are met. 
At onboarding, runtime policy activation:

Page | 29

• enforces declared governance constraints at defined enforcement points; 
• ensures governance decisions operate concurrently with system execution; and 
• enables real-time detection of policy deviation or control failure. 
Runtime policy activation does not imply system maturity or stability. During early operation, 
policies may be adaptive, conservative, and subject to frequent refinement. Governance 
effectiveness at this stage is evaluated by observed control behavior, not by absence of 
incidents.

6.3 Escalation and revocation during early operation 
Early operation is characterized by uncertainty. Accordingly, escalation and revocation 
mechanisms shall be treated as first-class controls during onboarding. 
During this phase: 
• escalation thresholds shall be conservative and explicit; 
• human-in-the-loop intervention shall be readily available; 
• governance decisions shall be traceable and reviewable; and 
• revocation or degradation of trust signals shall be expected governance outcomes, not 
exceptions. 
Revocation during onboarding is not punitive. It is a protective response indicating that 
assumptions have been invalidated or that evidence is insufficient to sustain prior trust claims. 
Access PoD ensures that escalation and revocation are operational actions, not retrospective 
judgments, allowing containment to remain effective as conditions evolve.

6.4 What onboarding does not certify or approve 
Version C explicitly constrains the interpretation of onboarding activities. Onboarding under 
Access PoD does not: 
• certify system safety, alignment, or compliance; 
• approve deployment, scale-up, or fitness for purpose; 
• grant regulatory endorsement or legal standing; 
• assert alignment maturity; or 
• imply permanence of trust.

7. Relationship to Q-Pathformer 
(Informative) 
This section clarifies the relationship between the Volume 2 governance framework and Q-
Pathformer during onboarding. It explains how Q-Pathformer may be used as a reference 
onboarding substrate, why its use is optional, and how organizations may transition beyond 
reference implementations without altering governance authority or assurance semantics. 
Nothing in this section modifies the normative requirements defined elsewhere in Volume 2.

7.1 Q-Pathformer as an onboarding substrate 
Q-Pathformer may be used as an onboarding substrate to support early validation of runtime 
governance concepts under controlled conditions. In this role, Q-Pathformer provides a 
concrete execution environment in which containment mechanisms— such as enforcement 
points, telemetry generation, and escalation pathways— can be exercised and observed. 
As an onboarding substrate, Q-Pathformer is used to: 
• demonstrate how governance controls attach to execution boundaries; 
• support simulation-first containment and early runtime governance; 
• enable inspection and review of evidence continuity; and 
• facilitate standards and regulatory exploration without production-scale deployment. 
Use of Q-Pathformer at onboarding is intended to support learning and validation, not to 
establish normative requirements or preferred architectures.

7.2 Why Q-Pathformer is optional 
The Volume 2 governance framework is architecture-agnostic and model-provider-neutral. 
Accordingly, use of Q-Pathformer is not required for onboarding into runtime governance. 
Q-Pathformer is optional because: 
• governance authority resides in Version A mechanisms, not in any execution substrate; 
• containment and assurance depend on observability and control, not on specific 
architectures; and 
• equivalent execution boundaries may exist in diverse systems with different internal 
designs.

Organizations may onboard using alternative systems or platforms, provided that the readiness 
conditions defined in Sections 3–6 are met. No governance outcome, assurance interpretation, 
or conformance claim depends on the use of Q-Pathformer.
