7.3 Using reference systems without embedding authority 
Reference systems, including Q-Pathformer, shall not be treated as sources of governance 
authority, approval, or trust. 
When used during onboarding: 
• reference systems illustrate feasibility, not compliance; 
• governance decisions remain external and independent; 
• assurance signals are computed outside the execution substrate; and 
• execution environments do not interpret or assert trust. 
Embedding governance authority into reference systems would undermine portability, 
comparability, and interoperability. Version C therefore maintains a strict separation between 
governance intent, execution substrate, and assurance interpretation, consistent with 
Versions A and B.

7.4 Transitioning beyond reference implementations 
Onboarding using a reference system is not an end state. Organizations are expected to 
transition beyond reference implementations as governance capability matures and 
operational contexts evolve. 
Such transitions: 
• do not require redefinition of governance principles; 
• do not alter CSC semantics or scoring logic; and 
• do not imply loss of conformance or assurance continuity. 
Where execution substrates change, governance outcomes shall be reassessed through 
evidence, not inferred from prior association with a reference system. Trust remains 
conditional on current observability, containment, and evidence quality, regardless of the 
platform in use. 
This approach ensures that governance scales with system evolution while remaining 
independent of any single technology or implementation.

8. Regulator and Standards Engagement During Onboarding 
This section describes how regulators and standards bodies may engage with and observe 
onboarding activities under the Volume 2 governance framework. It clarifies what may 
reasonably be observed at different onboarding phases, how evidence expectations evolve with 
governance maturity, and how misinterpretation of onboarding as certification is explicitly 
avoided. 
Engagement during onboarding is intended to support informed oversight and standards 
exploration, not to substitute for sector-specific regulatory processes or legal determinations.

8.1 What regulators can observe at each phase 
Regulatory and standards engagement during onboarding is necessarily phase-dependent, 
reflecting system maturity and governance readiness. 
For under-defined systems, regulators may observe: 
• simulation-based risk discovery activities; 
• declared execution boundaries and enforcement intent; 
• existence of escalation and human oversight pathways; and 
• evidence that onboarding is constrained and exploratory. 
At this phase, regulators should not expect stable assurance outputs or claims of alignment 
maturity. 
For informally defined systems, regulators may observe: 
• active runtime governance controls at declared enforcement points; 
• continuous telemetry generation and attribution; 
• provisional assurance signals, where present, clearly marked as such; and 
• documented responses to elevated-risk events or control deviations. 
For over-defined systems, regulators may observe: 
• sustained evidence continuity across lifecycle events; 
• stable application of runtime controls; 
• continuous assurance outputs derived from telemetry; and 
• observable degradation or revocation of trust where evidence warrants. 
At no phase does onboarding itself constitute regulatory approval or compliance 
determination.

8.2 Evidence expectations at entry vs maturity 
Evidence expectations evolve as systems progress through onboarding phases. Version C 
distinguishes clearly between entry evidence and maturity evidence. 
At entry: 
• evidence demonstrates containment capability; 
• telemetry may be incomplete but must be attributable; 
• assurance outputs, if any, are provisional; and 
• human oversight is central. 
At maturity: 
• evidence supports continuous assurance; 
• telemetry is stable, complete, and lifecycle-aware; 
• trust signals are continuously recalculated; and 
• governance responses to drift are observable. 
This distinction prevents premature assurance claims and supports proportionate oversight 
aligned to system maturity.

8.3 Avoiding certification-by-association 
A recurring risk during onboarding is certification-by-association, whereby participation in 
governance frameworks, pilot programs, or standards exploration is misinterpreted as 
endorsement or approval. 
Version C explicitly rejects certification-by-association. Accordingly: 
• onboarding activities shall not be represented as regulatory approval; 
• use of reference systems shall not imply compliance; 
• provisional assurance outputs shall not be marketed as certification; and 
• standards engagement shall not be conflated with conformance claims. 
Where misrepresentation occurs, trust signals shall be constrained or withdrawn until 
corrective clarification is made.

8.4 Cross-border and multi-sector considerations 
AI systems frequently operate across jurisdictions and sectors, each with distinct regulatory 
expectations and risk tolerances. Onboarding must therefore remain context-aware and 
adaptable. 
During onboarding: 
• sector-specific risk profiles shall be declared where applicable; 
• jurisdictional scope of evidence shall be explicit; 
• assurance interpretation shall be bounded by declared context; and 
• cross-border deployments shall not assume uniform regulatory acceptance. 
Standards bodies may use onboarding observations to inform guidance development, but such 
observations do not override sectoral or jurisdictional requirements. 
This approach supports interoperability of governance evidence while preserving regulatory 
sovereignty.

9. Failure Modes and Anti-Patterns 
This section identifies common failure modes and governance anti-patterns observed during 
AI system onboarding. These failures do not arise from malicious intent; they arise from 
misinterpretation, shortcutting, or overextension of governance concepts beyond what 
operational evidence can support. 
Version C explicitly documents these patterns to prevent misuse of the framework and to 
reinforce the principle that trust must be earned through containment and evidence, not 
inferred from participation or intent.

9.1 Treating onboarding as approval 
A primary failure mode is treating onboarding into a governance framework as an implicit form 
of approval, certification, or deployment readiness. 
Onboarding establishes eligibility for governed observation, not endorsement. When 
onboarding is misrepresented as approval: 
• risk is obscured rather than managed; 
• scrutiny is reduced at the point of highest uncertainty; and 
• accountability becomes diffused. 
This framework explicitly rejects onboarding-as-approval. Any representation of onboarding as 
certification, compliance, or regulatory endorsement constitutes a governance failure.

9.2 Confusing alignment claims with containment 
Another common anti-pattern is asserting alignment claims in the absence of operational 
containment. 
Alignment describes the consistency of system behavior with human, legal, and societal intent 
over time. Containment describes the ability to govern behavior while the system is running. 
When alignment is claimed without containment: 
• behavior cannot be continuously verified; 
• drift and misuse may go undetected; 
• and confidence becomes narrative-driven rather than evidence-based.

This framework treats containment as a prerequisite for meaningful alignment evaluation. 
Alignment without containment is not a sign of maturity; it is a source of false confidence.

9.3 Telemetry gaps at entry 
Telemetry gaps at onboarding represent a critical failure condition. 
Where governance-relevant telemetry is incomplete, delayed, or non-attributable: 
• assurance claims cannot be sustained; 
• escalation decisions lack evidentiary basis; and 
• trust signals, if present, are misleading. 
Telemetry gaps shall not be excused as temporary implementation limitations. At onboarding, 
incomplete telemetry must result in constrained operation and provisional trust, not implicit 
acceptance. 
9.4 Governance theatre 
Governance theatre occurs when governance artifacts, committees, or declarations exist 
without operational effect. 
Examples include: 
• policies that are not enforceable at runtime; 
• assurance statements unsupported by telemetry; 
• oversight bodies without escalation authority; and 
• documentation substituting for evidence. 
Governance theatre creates the appearance of control while masking real risk. Within this 
framework, governance that does not alter system behavior under real conditions is not 
governance— it is performative compliance. 
Normative Summary (Section 9) 
• Onboarding shall not be treated as approval or certification. 
• Alignment claims without containment are invalid. 
• Telemetry gaps at entry constitute governance failure. 
• Governance without operational effect is governance theatre. 
• Trust shall not be asserted without evidence.

10. Transition to Continuous Governance 
This section describes how organizations move from onboarding under Version C to steady-
state governance under Version A, and how future extensions may be introduced without 
disrupting governance authority or assurance semantics. 
Version C is transitional by design. Its role concludes once containment, evidence continuity, 
and operational discipline are sufficient to support continuous assurance.

10.1 From onboarding to steady-state 
The transition from onboarding to steady-state governance occurs when runtime governance 
mechanisms operate reliably under normal and stressed conditions. 
Indicators that an organization is ready to transition include: 
• sustained operation of runtime controls at declared enforcement points; 
• continuous, attributable telemetry across lifecycle events; 
• effective escalation and intervention under elevated-risk conditions; and 
• evidence that trust degradation or revocation has occurred appropriately when 
assumptions failed. 
At this point, governance emphasis shifts from entry discipline to ongoing assurance 
maintenance. Simulation, runtime enforcement, and evidence interpretation continue, but 
onboarding constraints are relaxed in favor of continuous evaluation. 
Steady-state governance does not imply reduced scrutiny. It reflects improved governance 
capability and confidence grounded in evidence rather than assumption.

10.2 When Version C hands back to Version A 
Version C hands back authority to Version A when onboarding considerations no longer 
dominate governance decisions. 
At that point: 
• governance intent, assurance semantics, and CSC scoring are governed exclusively by 
Version A;

Conclusion 
Governance as a lived capability 
Version C positions governance not as a static requirement or one-time assessment, but as a 
lived operational capability. Effective AI governance is demonstrated through continuous 
containment, evidence generation, and accountable intervention— not through declarations of 
intent or compliance artifacts alone. 
By formalizing onboarding as a governed transition, Version C enables organizations to enter 
runtime governance without asserting trust prematurely, while preserving the integrity of the 
framework defined in Version A.

Why containment enables alignment 
Alignment cannot be meaningfully evaluated without containment. Claims of alignment depend 
on whether system behavior can be constrained, observed, and corrected under real operating 
conditions. 
Version C reinforces that containment precedes alignment. It establishes the conditions under 
which alignment may strengthen over time— through governance maturity, operational 
learning, and specialization across policy, engineering, and oversight roles. Alignment improves 
not because systems are assumed to be safe, but because governance is capable of responding 
when they are not.

Why onboarding is the most fragile phase 
Onboarding is the point of greatest uncertainty and the highest risk of false confidence. It is 
where intent first meets execution, and where governance failure is most likely to be masked 
by documentation, reputation, or optimism. 
Version C treats onboarding as a fragile but necessary phase, requiring explicit discipline, 
constrained trust, and heightened oversight. By doing so, it prevents governance shortcuts and 
ensures that trust, once earned, remains grounded in evidence rather than assumption.

Canonical paper: 
APOD-TR-005_Vol2_Version-D (PDF)

v1d-Governance Stress Testing and Ethical Evaluation

https://github.com/Access-PoD/access-pod-artifacts/releases/tag/v1d

Overview 
Version D extends the A WEB of Sharing Trust–Responsibility Toward a Trustless Future 
platform by introducing structured governance stress-testing and ethical evaluation. 
While earlier editions establish governance authority (Version A), demonstrate execution-level 
feasibility (Version B), and formalize onboarding and containment (Version C), Version D 
addresses a critical unresolved question: 
How does governance behave when it is deliberately stressed before harm occurs? 
Version D treats governance itself as a system under load, and ethics as a decision capability 
exercised under uncertainty, rather than as a checklist, alignment label, or certification claim.

What This Release Introduces 
Version D introduces a disciplined, non-exploitative approach to governance stress-testing, 
including: 
• Defined governance stress categories, such as: 
o authority stress, 
o delegation stress, 
o telemetry stress, 
o incentive stress, and 
o ethical ambiguity stress. 
• Non-exploitative stress-testing methods, grounded in simulation, walkthroughs, and 
revocation rehearsal rather than adversarial hacking or red-team activity. 
• A clear treatment of ethics under governance stress, focusing on responsibility, 
restraint, escalation, and non-decision under uncertainty. 
• Formal rules for how stress-testing evidence may constrain trust and assurance, 
without modifying or extending Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) semantics.

Page | 3

• Explicit guardrails preventing stress-testing-as-certification, benchmarking, or 
marketing misuse. 
Stress-testing failures are treated as valuable governance evidence, not defects to be 
concealed or reframed.

Relationship to the v1.0-Workshop 
Effective use of Version D presumes the human governance capability developed through the 
v1.0-workshop — Designing Governance-Ready AI Outputs. 
The workshop is represented in two complementary forms. The public workshop repository 
contains Markdown-based materials intended for inspection, versioning, and standards-
adjacent review. The workshop information pack published on the website provides a 
structured overview of the workshop’s purpose, scope, and learning outcomes for prospective 
participants. 
These serve different audiences and functions: the repository supports technical and 
governance transparency, while the website materials support orientation and engagement 
without conveying governance authority or certification. 
The workshop develops disciplined professional practice in: 
• articulating governance intent and scope, 
• identifying non-delegable judgment, 
• reasoning under uncertainty, 
• documenting defensible decisions, and 
• exercising escalation and non-decision responsibly. 
Without this human capability substrate, governance stress-testing risks becoming abstract or 
performative. With it, Version D becomes practical, accountable, and decision-relevant.

Stress-testing evidence interacts with assurance only by constraint. It may narrow scope, justify 
provisional assurance, or rehearse revocation readiness, but it cannot elevate trust signals or 
justify deployment. Trust that cannot degrade under stress is not trustworthy. 
Version D is intended for regulators, standards bodies, system operators, boards, and risk 
committees at governance inflection points - such as prior to scale-up, scope expansion, or 
integration into higher-impact contexts. It is not intended for public benchmarking, marketing 
claims, or certification-by-association. 
Effective use of Version D presumes the human governance capabilities developed through the 
v1.0-workshop, which provides the reasoning discipline required to articulate boundaries, own 
accountability, and act under uncertainty. Without this human substrate, governance stress-
testing risks becoming abstract or performative.

• Version A defines governance authority and assurance semantics. 
• Version B demonstrates execution-level feasibility.

• v1.0-workshop develops the human capability required to exercise all of the above

withdrawn before impact occurs.

Chapter 1 — Why Governance Must Be Stress-Tested 
1.1 The Limits of Nominal Governance 
AI governance frameworks are typically evaluated under nominal conditions: 
stable assumptions, cooperative actors, intact telemetry, and aligned incentives. 
Under such conditions, governance mechanisms often appear sufficient. Policies are 
documented, controls are declared, escalation paths exist on paper, and ethical principles are 
articulated clearly. 
However, nominal conditions are not where governance fails. 
Governance failures emerge when: 
• incentives conflict with stated controls, 
• uncertainty increases beyond expected bounds, 
• accountability becomes inconvenient, 
• evidence is incomplete or contested, or 
• human intervention carries cost or delay. 
Existing governance approaches rarely test these conditions explicitly. As a result, they risk 
mistaking designed intent for operational resilience. 
Version D addresses this gap by treating governance not as a static construct, but as a system 
that must withstand stress before it can be trusted.

1.2 Governance as a System Under Load 
In mature engineering disciplines, systems are not evaluated solely by design documentation or 
nominal performance. They are stress-tested to observe behavior under adverse or extreme 
conditions. 
Examples include: 
• financial stress testing to assess capital adequacy under market shock, 
• safety-case challenge scenarios in aviation and nuclear systems, 
• disaster recovery drills in critical infrastructure. 
These practices do not assume failure is exceptional. They assume failure is informative. 
AI governance, by contrast, is often evaluated only by:

Page | 12

• whether policies exist, 
• whether documentation is complete, 
• whether principles are declared. 
This creates a structural blind spot: 
governance is rarely observed while it is being strained. 
Version D treats governance mechanisms - policies, escalation logic, human-in-the-loop 
controls, assurance signals - as systems that must perform under load, not merely exist in 
specification.

2.1 Why Governance Stress Must Be Categorized 
Governance stress does not manifest as a single condition. It emerges through distinct pressure

• systematic evaluation across systems and sectors, 
• comparable interpretation of outcomes, 
• and targeted refinement of controls. 
Version D therefore defines a set of governance stress categories. These categories do not 
correspond to technical faults or security exploits; they correspond to decision pressure points 
where governance assumptions are most likely to fail.

2.2 Authority Stress 
Who decides when governance becomes inconvenient 
Authority stress occurs when governance decision rights are unclear, contested, or bypassed

Typical triggers include: 
• urgent operational deadlines, 
• conflicting internal stakeholders, 
• external commercial or political pressure, 
• escalation fatigue or perceived “over-governance.”

• decision ownership becomes ambiguous, 
• escalation is deferred or diluted, 
• or authority is informally reassigned without traceability. 
Stress-testing authority examines whether: 
• governance authority remains explicit under time pressure, 
• escalation pathways are exercised rather than bypassed,

• assurance signals are constrained rather than asserted,

Telemetry stress distinguishes evidence-based governance from evidence-optional governance.

2.5 Incentive Stress

Governance systems operate within organizations that also pursue:

• competitive advantage, 
• reputational positioning. 
Incentive stress occurs when these goals conflict with governance constraints. 
Common scenarios include: 
• pressure to deploy despite unresolved risk, 
• reluctance to trigger revocation or downgrade signals, 
• framing governance outcomes to preserve optics. 
Stress-testing incentives examines whether: 
• governance controls withstand commercial or reputational pressure, 
• assurance mechanisms remain neutral under success narratives, 
• and ethical considerations are not subordinated to short-term gain.

Not all ethical risks are immediate, measurable, or catastrophic. 
Ethical ambiguity stress arises when:

Stress-testing ethical ambiguity examines whether:

• governance allows for precautionary intervention, 
• and responsibility is acknowledged despite uncertainty.

Chapter 3 — Governance Stress-Testing Methods (Non-Exploitative) 
3.1 Why Stress-Testing Methods Must Be Constrained 
Stress-testing governance introduces a paradox: 
• If stress is applied too lightly, failures remain hidden. 
• If stress is applied too aggressively, testing itself becomes unsafe, unethical, or 
misleading. 
Version D therefore requires explicitly bounded stress-testing methods. These methods are 
designed to: 
• reveal governance weaknesses, 
• preserve system safety, 
• protect third-party interests, and 
• avoid creating new risk during evaluation. 
Stress-testing governance is not an adversarial contest. It is a controlled inquiry into decision 
behavior under pressure.

All stress-testing activities under Version D shall conform to the following principles: 
1. Non-exploitative by design 
Stress-testing shall not involve vulnerability exploitation, security bypass, or

The object of stress is governance behavior, not model internals or performance 
characteristics.

All stress scenarios must remain reviewable, interruptible, and attributable to human 
decision authority. 
4. Reversible impact 
Stress-testing shall not cause irreversible system changes, data corruption, or real-world 
harm. 
5. Evidence-generating, not judgment-issuing

ethical scores.

Simulation AI-Powered Policies (SAPP), introduced in Version A, provide the primary 
mechanism for pre-impact stress testing. 
Under Version D, SAPP is used to simulate conditions that: 
• increase uncertainty, 
• challenge governance assumptions, 
• or expose boundary ambiguity. 
Examples include: 
• simulated policy conflicts, 
• adversarial but non-exploitative user behavior, 
• escalation saturation scenarios, 
• delegation chains under constrained oversight. 
Simulation allows governance to be stressed without exposing real users, markets, or 
infrastructure.

reveal how governance responds, not to forecast harm. 
In regulatory and supervisory contexts, this class of simulation aligns with emerging regtech 
approaches that test governance behaviour and decision pathways before live system 
exposure, rather than relying on post-incident reporting or retrospective audits.

Chapter 4 — Ethics Under Governance Stress 
4.1 Why Ethics Emerges Only Under Pressure 
Ethical intent is often articulated at design time, when choices are abstract and consequences 
are distant. Under these conditions, ethical positions tend to converge and appear 
uncontroversial. 
Ethical reality, however, emerges under pressure, when decisions must be made with 
incomplete information, competing obligations, and tangible consequences. 
Version D therefore treats ethics not as a static alignment state, but as a governance function 
exercised under stress. Ethics is revealed by how decisions are made when: 
• evidence is ambiguous, 
• harm is plausible but not yet realized, 
• intervention carries cost or delay, and 
• responsibility cannot be deferred to procedure. 
Ethics that cannot be exercised under these conditions is not operational ethics.

4.2 Ethics as a Governance Capability, Not a Principle Set 
Many ethical frameworks emphasize principles such as fairness, accountability, transparency, 
and human oversight. While these principles are necessary, they do not determine who 
decides, when to intervene, or how to act under uncertainty. 
Within Version D: 
• ethics is treated as a decision capability, 
• exercised through governance controls, 
• bounded by authority and accountability, 
• and evidenced through action and restraint. 
Ethics is therefore inseparable from governance structure. Where governance authority is 
unclear, ethical responsibility becomes diffuse. Where escalation is blocked, ethical intent 
becomes performative.

4.3 Ethical Authority and Non-Delegability 
A central ethical question in AI governance is whether ethical judgment can be delegated. 
Version D asserts that ethical judgment is non-delegable, even when AI systems assist with 
analysis, simulation, or drafting. 
Accordingly: 
• AI may surface ethical considerations but shall not resolve them. 
• Ethical trade-offs shall not be automated. 
• Responsibility for ethical decisions shall remain human, attributable, and defensible. 
Stress-testing ethics therefore examines whether governance mechanisms preserve ethical 
authority under pressure, rather than whether ethical principles are declared.

4.4 Ethical Decision-Making Under Uncertainty 
Ethical failure often occurs not through overt harm, but through delay, minimization, or 
normalization in the face of uncertainty. 
Common ethical stress conditions include: 
• uncertainty about affected populations, 
• indirect or long-term impacts, 
• competing interpretations of acceptable risk, 
• lack of definitive evidence. 
Version D does not require ethical certainty. It requires ethical containment. 
Ethical containment means: 
• the ability to pause or constrain operation, 
• explicit acknowledgment of uncertainty, 
• documentation of decision rationale, 
• willingness to escalate without proof of harm. 
Under Version D, ethical restraint is a valid and expected outcome.

4.5 The Ethics of “Not Deciding” 
One of the most under-examined ethical acts in AI governance is the decision not to decide. 
Non-decision may take the form of: 
• deferring deployment, 
• limiting scope, 
• suspending a capability, 
• requiring additional evidence before proceeding. 
Version D treats non-decision not as failure, but as a first-class ethical action when conditions 
do not justify progression. 
Stress-testing ethics therefore includes scenarios where the ethically defensible action is to: 
• halt, 
• slow, 
• or reverse. 
Governance systems that cannot support ethical non-decision are structurally biased toward 
action - even when action is unjustified.

4.6 Ethical Escalation and Accountability 
Ethical decisions under stress require escalation pathways that are: 
• explicit, 
• accessible, 
• and empowered. 
Version D examines whether ethical concerns can: 
• trigger escalation without stigma, 
• reach decision-makers with authority, 
• and result in proportional intervention. 
Ethical escalation is not whistleblowing. It is a designed governance pathway. 
Stress-testing ethics reveals whether ethical escalation is operational, or merely aspirational.

Chapter 5 — Evidence Produced by Governance Stress-Testing 
5.1 Why Stress-Testing Evidence Must Be Distinguished 
Governance stress-testing generates evidence that is qualitatively different from: 
• performance benchmarks, 
• security findings, 
• compliance artifacts, or 
• assurance certifications. 
If this distinction is not made explicit, stress-testing risks being misused to: 
• imply approval, 
• justify deployment, 
• or replace lifecycle assurance. 
Version D therefore defines stress-testing evidence as a specific class of governance evidence, 
with clear scope, limits, and interpretation rules.

5.2 What Counts as Governance Stress-Testing Evidence 
Under Version D, governance stress-testing produces evidence about governance behavior, not 
system correctness. 
Valid evidence types include: 
• Observed failure modes 
Where authority, escalation, or evidence handling degraded under stress. 
• Boundary clarifications 
Explicit identification of where governance assumptions broke or became ambiguous. 
• Decision rationales under pressure 
Documented reasoning for action, restraint, escalation, or non-decision. 
• Control responsiveness 
Whether governance mechanisms activated as designed when stressed. 
• Ethical constraint articulation 
How ethical uncertainty was handled, constrained, or escalated. 
This evidence reflects how governance behaves, not whether a system is “safe” or “aligned.”

To prevent misuse, Version D explicitly excludes the following interpretations:

• proof of safety or alignment,

• validation of readiness,

Stress-testing evidence must meet minimum quality standards to be meaningful:

Chapter 6 — Relationship to CSC, Trust, and Revocation 
6.1 Why Stress-Testing Must Constrain Trust, Not Inflate It 
Governance stress-testing is often misinterpreted as a way to increase confidence. 
Version D explicitly rejects this framing. 
Stress-testing exists to challenge trust assumptions, not to validate them. 
A governance system that performs well only under favorable conditions is not trustworthy, it is 
untested. 
Accordingly, stress-testing evidence may restrict, qualify, or delay trust signals, but it shall 
never be used to elevate trust status or justify deployment readiness.

6.2 CSC Authority Remains Defined Exclusively by Version A 
The Compliance Star Certificate (CSC) is defined entirely by Version A: 
• assurance semantics, 
• scoring logic, 
• evidence requirements, 
• degradation and revocation rules. 
Version D introduces no new CSC criteria, weights, star levels, or scoring pathways. 
Stress-testing outcomes do not: 
• increase CSC scores, 
• substitute for telemetry, 
• override CSC qualification gates, 
• or justify star-level progression. 
CSC authority remains unchanged and external to stress-testing activities.

6.3 How Stress-Testing Interacts with CSC (Constraint Path) 
Stress-testing affects CSC only through constraint, not computation. 
Valid interactions include:

Page | 38

• Scope limitation 
Stress-testing may reveal that assurance applies only to a narrower context than 
previously assumed. 
• Provisional qualification 
Unresolved stress-test failures may justify marking CSC outputs as provisional or 
exploratory. 
• Degradation readiness 
Stress-testing may identify conditions under which CSC degradation or revocation must 
be triggered rapidly. 
Stress-testing therefore functions as a trust boundary clarifier, not an assurance generator.

6.4 Stress-Testing as a Precursor to Revocation Readiness 
Version A defines revocation as a protective governance action, not a punitive one. 
Version D ensures that revocation is operationally realistic. 
Stress-testing examines whether: 
• revocation pathways exist, 
• revocation can be executed without institutional resistance, 
• trust signals can be degraded without narrative manipulation, 
• and accountability remains intact during rollback. 
A governance system that cannot rehearse revocation cannot credibly claim revocation 
readiness.

6.5 Trust Degradation as a Valid Outcome 
Under Version D, trust degradation is not a failure condition - it is an expected governance 
outcome. 
Stress-testing may legitimately result in: 
• constrained assurance, 
• reduced CSC scope, 
• downgraded star levels, 
• or temporary suspension of trust signals.

Page | 39

Attempting to preserve trust signals in the face of unresolved stress-test findings constitutes 
governance failure. 
Trust that cannot degrade cannot be trusted.

6.6 Stress-Testing and Lifecycle Governance 
Stress-testing evidence is time-bound and context-specific. 
Accordingly: 
• successful stress-testing does not confer permanent trust; 
• new stress conditions may invalidate prior findings; 
• system evolution may require re-entry into stress-testing. 
Version D therefore treats stress-testing as a recurring lifecycle activity, not a one-time gate. 
Stress-testing supports continuous governance by ensuring that trust claims remain 
conditioned on current behavior, not historical success.

A critical guardrail in Version D is the explicit prevention of stress-testing being misrepresented

Chapter 7 — Who Should Use Version D, and When 
7.1 Why Audience and Timing Matter 
Governance stress-testing is powerful precisely because it can surface uncomfortable truths. 
Used at the wrong time, or by the wrong actors, it can also be misapplied, misunderstood, or 
weaponized. 
Version D therefore defines who should use governance stress-testing, under what conditions, 
and for what purpose. This is not an access control mechanism; it is a use-discipline 
requirement intended to preserve governance integrity and standards credibility.

7.2 Intended Primary Users 
Version D is intended for actors who hold, influence, or evaluate governance authority, not for 
those seeking validation, benchmarking, or market signaling. 
Regulators and Oversight Bodies 
Regulators may use Version D to: 
• evaluate whether governance mechanisms remain credible under stress, 
• assess revocation readiness and escalation realism, 
• identify systemic governance blind spots before harm occurs. 
Version D does not provide regulatory approval criteria. It supports oversight literacy, not 
enforcement thresholds.

Standards Bodies and Technical Committees 
Standards organizations may use Version D to: 
• explore how governance frameworks behave under adverse conditions, 
• assess whether proposed standards support evidence-based trust under stress, 
• identify where standards language may fail to anticipate real-world governance 
pressure. 
Version D is suitable for standards exploration and stress-informed drafting, not for normative 
requirement setting.

Version D should be applied before confidence is asserted, not after incidents occur.

Boards, Risk Committees, and Executive Oversight 
Governance stress-testing is particularly relevant for decision-makers who must: 
• sign off on risk posture, 
• accept accountability for trust claims, 
• authorize expansion into new contexts or markets. 
For these actors, Version D provides a structured way to ask: 
“What happens to governance when things go wrong?”

7.3 When Version D Should Be Applied 
Version D is most appropriate at decision inflection points, including: 
• prior to deployment into higher-impact contexts, 
• before expanding scope, autonomy, or delegation, 
• when onboarding new models, tools, or data sources, 
• following material system changes, 
• when assurance signals appear stable but untested. 
It is not intended for continuous application during steady-state operation. 
It is a deliberate stress activity, not an always-on monitoring function.

To prevent misuse, Version D should not be applied: 
• as a public benchmarking exercise, 
• as a prerequisite for market access, 
• as a substitute for regulatory compliance, 
• as a red-team security activity, 
• as a marketing or signaling tool. 
Applying Version D in these contexts risks converting governance stress-testing into governance 
theatre or coercive evaluation, undermining its purpose.

Document Control Information 
Document Identifier: APOD-TR-006 
Title: A WEB of Sharing Trust–Responsibility Toward a Trustless Future Vol.2 
Edition: Second Edition — Version E 
Date of Issue: 5th February 2026 
Status: Draft (Standards Exploration — Method Paper) 
Author: Anthony Siljeg 
Affiliation: Alnotrea Labs / Policy of Developments — Access PoD Initiative

Abstract 
This paper introduces Access-Mode as a reasoning orchestration method for AI-assisted 
governance work. It addresses a persistent failure mode observed in practice: the unintentional 
mixing of learning, operational, and inspection reasoning when AI systems interact with 
governance materials. Such mixing produces ambiguity, over-confidence, and misuse of 
otherwise well-designed governance artifacts.

Version E formalizes Access-Mode as a non-normative, model-agnostic control layer that 
governs reasoning posture at the project level. It defines explicit reasoning modes, rules for 
controlled cross-mode use, and human-in-the-loop validation practices, including intentional 
misalignment testing as an error-detection method for high-impact outputs.

Access-Mode does not assert correctness, compliance, or deployment readiness. Instead, it 
complements existing workshop, workspace, and artifact-based governance releases by 
ensuring that AI-assisted reasoning remains interpretable, bounded, and reviewable. This paper 
is intended to support standards exploration, reviewer interpretation, and disciplined use of AI 
systems in governance contexts. 
This document is informative and methodological. It does not define requirements, controls, or 
conformance criteria.

Overview 
Version E addresses a recurring challenge that emerges as governance tooling and AI capability 
increase: 
When learning, operational analysis, and inspection reasoning are not explicitly separated, AI-
assisted outputs can appear fluent while obscuring uncertainty, intent, and responsibility. 
Access-Mode responds by: 
• defining three explicit reasoning modes (ID_1, ID_2, ID_3), 
• enforcing primary and secondary mode discipline at the project level, and 
• introducing validation practices that expose reasoning fragility without asserting 
correctness or trust. 
This edition treats reasoning itself as a governable activity, without redefining governance 
authority or outcomes.

What Version E Introduces 
Version E introduces: 
• A non-normative, model-agnostic Access-Mode method for reasoning orchestration. 
• Explicit separation of: 
o learning (ID_1), 
o operational / runtime analysis (ID_2), 
o inspection and review reasoning (ID_3). 
• Project-level reasoning boundaries and session stability rules.

1. Introduction 
1.1 Purpose of Version E 
The purpose of Version E is to formalize Access-Mode as a reasoning orchestration method for 
AI-assisted governance work. 
Previous versions of this series established: 
• governance authority and assurance semantics (Version A), 
• execution-level feasibility (Version B), 
• onboarding and containment discipline (Version C), and 
• governance and ethical stress-testing (Version D). 
Version E addresses a different class of problem: 
how AI systems reason when interacting with governance materials, and how that reasoning 
can be disciplined without asserting compliance, correctness, or trust. 
This paper defines Access-Mode as a method for controlling reasoning posture, ensuring that 
learning, operational analysis, and inspection are not unintentionally conflated when AI systems 
are used to support governance activities. Version E also formalizes validation and error-
detection practices required to interpret AI-generated governance reasoning safely

1.2 The Problem Addressed by Access-Mode 
In practice, AI systems are increasingly used to: 
• explain governance concepts, 
• analyze operational scenarios, 
• and prepare materials for review or standards discussion. 
However, these activities require fundamentally different reasoning postures. 
Without explicit controls, AI systems tend to: 
• merge explanatory and operational language, 
• introduce inspection-style certainty into exploratory analysis, or 
• treat illustrative artifacts as authoritative. 
This phenomenon— referred to in this paper as reasoning mode collapse— results in: 
• ambiguity,

Page | 10

• over-confidence, 
• and misuse of otherwise well-designed governance artifacts. 
Version E addresses this gap by introducing reasoning orchestration as a first-class governance 
concern.

1.3 Access-Mode in Relation to Existing Governance Constructs 
Access-Mode does not replace existing governance frameworks, artifacts, or tools. 
Instead, it operates above them, governing how reasoning occurs when those materials are 
used by AI systems. 
Access-Mode is: 
• model-agnostic, 
• architecture-independent, and 
• non-normative. 
It does not define new governance requirements. 
It defines how AI systems should reason within existing governance boundaries.

1.4 Relationship to Access Policy-on-Demand (Access PoD) 
Access-Mode is conceptually aligned with Access Policy-on-Demand (Access PoD), but they 
address different layers of the governance problem. 
• Access PoD governs execution and enforcement at runtime, using policy-as-code, 
simulation, and telemetry. 
• Access-Mode governs reasoning posture, ensuring that AI systems interpret and use 
governance materials appropriately. 
In environments where Access PoD is present, Access-Mode may be used to: 
• control how AI systems reason about policy inputs, 
• distinguish between exploratory analysis and enforceable logic, and 
• prevent AI-generated outputs from being mistaken for execution-level signals. 
Access-Mode does not require Access PoD to function. 
It remains valid in governance contexts where Access PoD is not deployed.

Access-Mode is designed to operate across multiple industry contexts without embedding 
industry-specific assumptions into the reasoning process. 
Where Access PoD is used, governance execution may be structured around six operating 
factors (for example: authority, scope, control, evidence, escalation, and accountability). These 
factors influence runtime inputs and outputs within Access PoD. 
Access-Mode does not redefine these factors. 
Instead, it ensures that AI reasoning about them remains: 
• appropriately scoped, 
• mode-consistent (learning, operational, or inspection),

• inputs and outputs may flow through multiple governance modules,

This separation allows: 
• industry-specific execution to vary, while 
• reasoning discipline remains stable.

2. The Governance Reasoning Problem 
2.1 AI-Assisted Governance as a Cognitive System 
When AI systems are used to support governance work, they function as cognitive systems, not 
passive tools. 
They: 
• synthesize information, 
• reframe language, 
• infer relationships, and 
• project confidence through fluent output. 
In governance contexts, this cognitive amplification directly affects: 
• how intent is interpreted, 
• how risk is framed, 
• and how accountability is perceived. 
As a result, the behavior of the AI system’s reasoning becomes part of the governance system 
itself, even when no execution or enforcement occurs.

2.2 Failure Modes in Prompt-Only AI Use 
Most AI-assisted governance work relies on prompt-only interaction. 
Prompt-only use assumes that: 
• intent can be fully specified in natural language, 
• the AI will maintain consistent reasoning boundaries across interactions, and 
• users will notice when posture changes occur. 
In practice, these assumptions rarely hold. 
Prompt-only systems tend to: 
• optimize locally for the most recent instruction, 
• implicitly fill gaps when information is missing, and 
• shift tone and certainty without signaling the change. 
This leads to outputs that appear coherent but lack stable reasoning posture.

2.3 Reasoning Mode Collapse 
A common failure pattern observed in AI-assisted governance is reasoning mode collapse. 
Mode collapse occurs when: 
• explanatory language (learning), 
• exploratory analysis (operational), and 
• review-oriented framing (inspection) 
are merged into a single response. 
When this happens, the AI may: 
• explain a concept, 
• speculate about its runtime behavior, and 
• present the result in inspection-style language, 
without making the transitions explicit. 
This collapse is particularly dangerous in governance work because it produces: 
• unjustified certainty, 
• ambiguous authority, 
• and outputs that are difficult to challenge or review.

2.4 Over-Confidence and Interpretability Loss 
Large language models are optimized for fluency and coherence. 
In governance contexts, this fluency can be misinterpreted as: 
• correctness, 
• completeness, or 
• endorsement. 
As reasoning modes collapse, outputs may: 
• sound definitive without being grounded, 
• blur exploratory and authoritative statements, and

Page | 15

• suppress uncertainty rather than expose it. 
This results in interpretability loss, where reviewers cannot easily determine: 
• what assumptions were made, 
• which sources were relied upon, or 
• which conclusions are provisional.

2.5 Misuse of Governance Artifacts by AI Systems 
Governance artifacts— such as policies, frameworks, and standards drafts— are authored with 
human judgment in mind. 
They often rely on: 
• contextual interpretation, 
• implicit professional norms, and 
• staged reasoning across time. 
When AI systems consume these artifacts without reasoning controls, they tend to: 
• recombine clauses across contexts, 
• treat illustrative examples as prescriptive, 
• or infer obligations where none are stated. 
This misuse is not a failure of the artifacts themselves, but a failure to control how reasoning is 
applied to them.

2.6 Why This Problem Cannot Be Solved by Better Prompts Alone 
Improving prompts can reduce some errors, but it does not solve the underlying problem. 
Prompting operates at the message level. 
Governance reasoning failures occur at the session and project level. 
Without persistent controls, even well-crafted prompts: 
• decay over time, 
• are overridden by later instructions, or 
• are silently reinterpreted by the model.

Page | 16

This makes prompt-only mitigation insufficient for high-impact governance work.

If unaddressed, governance reasoning failures can lead to: 
• misplaced trust in AI-generated outputs, 
• inappropriate reuse of draft material, 
• and erosion of accountability. 
For standards bodies, regulators, and governance practitioners, this creates a critical gap: 
governance artifacts may be correct, but the reasoning applied to them is not controlled. 
Access-Mode is introduced in response to this gap.

3. Positioning Access-Mode 
3.1 Access-Mode as a Method, Not a Framework 
Access-Mode is defined in this paper as a method for reasoning orchestration, not as a 
governance framework, architecture, or artifact set. 
A framework typically: 
• defines concepts and structures, 
• enumerates principles or controls, and 
• may imply progression or maturity. 
Access-Mode does none of these. 
Instead, Access-Mode defines how reasoning is conducted when AI systems are used in 
governance contexts. It constrains reasoning posture without introducing new governance 
semantics, requirements, or authority. 
This distinction is intentional. Access-Mode is designed to operate alongside existing 
frameworks, not to compete with or replace them.

3.2 Distinction from Compliance, Certification, and Assurance 
Access-Mode does not assert: 
• compliance, 
• certification, 
• assurance, 
• readiness, 
• or correctness. 
It does not evaluate systems, organizations, or outcomes. 
Where compliance and assurance frameworks ask: 
• “Does this meet a defined requirement?” 
Access-Mode asks: 
• “What kind of reasoning is being applied here?”

3.3 Access-Mode and Human-Centric Governance 
Governance decisions remain the responsibility of humans. 
Access-Mode is explicitly designed to: 
• preserve human judgment, 
• surface assumptions rather than conceal them, and 
• make AI-assisted reasoning inspectable. 
By enforcing clear reasoning postures, Access-Mode: 
• prevents AI systems from projecting unwarranted authority, 
• supports deliberation rather than automation, and 
• aligns AI assistance with professional governance practice. 
Access-Mode therefore reinforces, rather than weakens, human-centric governance.

3.4 Why Reasoning Orchestration Is Required 
As shown in Chapter 2, failures in AI-assisted governance arise not from missing artifacts, but 
from uncontrolled reasoning behavior. 
Reasoning orchestration is required because: 
• governance work spans different cognitive activities, 
• AI systems do not inherently signal posture changes, and 
• humans may misinterpret fluent outputs as authoritative. 
Without orchestration, learning, operational analysis, and inspection reasoning are easily 
conflated. 
Access-Mode addresses this by: 
• explicitly defining reasoning postures, 
• enforcing posture persistence across sessions, and 
• preventing silent transitions between modes.

4. The Access-Mode Method 
4.1 Definition of Reasoning Postures 
The Access-Mode method is based on the concept of a reasoning posture. 
A reasoning posture defines: 
• the type of cognitive activity being performed, 
• the assumptions that are permitted, 
• the level of certainty that may be expressed, and 
• the kinds of conclusions that are allowed. 
In governance contexts, different activities require different postures. Explaining a concept, 
analyzing operational behavior, and preparing material for inspection are not interchangeable 
tasks, even when they draw on the same underlying artifacts. 
Access-Mode formalizes these postures so that AI-assisted reasoning remains explicit and 
interpretable.

4.2 Primary and Secondary Mode Discipline 
At the core of the Access-Mode method is the distinction between primary and secondary 
modes. 
• The primary mode defines the authoritative reasoning posture for a session or project. 
• A secondary mode, if allowed, may provide limited support or perspective. 
Only one primary mode may be active at any time. 
Secondary modes: 
• may clarify, 
• may reframe, 
• or may surface implications, 
but they must never override the assumptions, tone, or conclusions permitted by the primary 
mode. 
This discipline prevents silent escalation of authority and ensures that reasoning intent remains 
stable.

Access-Mode is enforced at the project level, not at the individual prompt level.

• which reasoning posture is primary,

• reduces drift, 
• supports consistent interpretation, and

4.5 Mixed-Mode Handling (Method Overview) 
Terminology note: 
The term “mixed-mode” is used in this paper to describe projects in which more than one 
reasoning posture is present. Although such projects permit only one primary and one 
constrained secondary mode, they are described as mixed-mode to emphasize the introduction 
of reasoning-boundary risk and the need for explicit control. Secondary modes are never 
equivalent to the primary mode. 
In limited cases, governance work benefits from controlled secondary reasoning. 
The Access-Mode method permits mixed-mode reasoning only when: 
• a single primary mode is clearly defined, and 
• secondary use is explicitly constrained. 
Mixed-mode handling is not implicit. It must be: 
• declared, 
• bounded, and 
• documented. 
The mechanics of mixed-mode control are described in Chapter 6. At the method level, the key 
principle is that supporting perspectives do not become governing perspectives.

4.6 Human Responsibility Within the Method 
Access-Mode does not remove or dilute human responsibility. 
Humans are responsible for: 
• selecting the appropriate primary mode, 
• determining whether secondary reasoning is allowed, 
• monitoring for posture drift, and 
• deciding when to stop or reset a session. 
The method is designed to support human judgment, not replace it. 
Where ambiguity arises, the correct response is not to refine prompts further, but to reassess 
the reasoning posture being applied.

5.1 Purpose of Mode Formalization 
The Access-Mode method defines three distinct reasoning modes. 
Each mode represents a different cognitive posture, not a different level of maturity, 
capability, or authority. 
The purpose of formalizing these modes is to: 
• prevent unintentional mixing of reasoning styles, 
• make AI-assisted governance reasoning interpretable, and 
• preserve human accountability across different governance activities. 
Only one Access-Mode is primary at any time.

5.2 Mode ID_1 — Foundational (Learning) Reasoning 
Method Definition 
Mode ID_1 defines a foundational reasoning posture. 
It is used when the objective is to: 
• understand concepts, 
• clarify intent and scope, 
• align terminology, and 
• reason about governance meaning without operational assumptions. 
ID_1 treats all governance artifacts as conceptual references, not as executable or inspectable

Permitted Reasoning Characteristics 
ID_1 allows reasoning that is: 
• explanatory, 
• descriptive, 
• scope-aware, and 
• provisional.

Page | 26

Outputs in this mode may: 
• explore definitions, 
• surface assumptions, 
• and restate intent.

Explicit Constraints 
ID_1 does not permit: 
• runtime behavior analysis, 
• enforcement or telemetry assumptions, 
• inspection or audit conclusions, 
• or statements of adequacy or sufficiency. 
If such reasoning is required, the method requires transition to another mode.

5.3 Mode ID_2 — Operational (Runtime) Reasoning 
Method Definition 
Mode ID_2 defines an operational reasoning posture. 
It is used when the objective is to: 
• explore governance behavior under use, 
• examine stress, failure, or drift, 
• and reason about uncertainty in execution contexts. 
ID_2 assumes that a system is operating or could operate, but it does not assert that operation 
is safe, correct, or compliant.

Permitted Reasoning Characteristics 
ID_2 allows reasoning that is: 
• scenario-based, 
• conditional,

Page | 27

• uncertainty-aware, and 
• exploratory. 
Outputs in this mode may: 
• describe “what-if” conditions, 
• identify failure modes, 
• and surface governance fragility.

Explicit Constraints 
ID_2 does not permit: 
• certification or approval language, 
• conclusions of compliance, 
• final judgments of adequacy, 
• or replacement of human decision-making. 
Operational reasoning remains provisional by design.

The three Access-Modes are not progressive stages. 
They do not represent: 
• increasing maturity, 
• increasing trust, 
• or escalation toward approval. 
Each mode answers a different question: 
• ID_1: What does this mean? 
• ID_2: What happens under pressure? 
• ID_3: How will this be interpreted or reviewed? 
Treating these modes as interchangeable or hierarchical undermines governance clarity.

6. Cross-Mode Reasoning Rules 
6.1 Purpose of Cross-Mode Rules 
Cross-mode reasoning rules exist to prevent reasoning ambiguity when AI systems are used to 
support governance work across different cognitive postures. 
AI systems can easily blur: 
• learning explanations, 
• operational analysis, and 
• inspection-style conclusions. 
These rules ensure that: 
• reasoning posture remains explicit, 
• authority is not silently escalated, and 
• outputs remain interpretable and reviewable by humans. 
Cross-mode rules govern controlled interaction between a primary reasoning posture and a 
constrained secondary posture; they do not imply equal or interchangeable modes.

6.2 Core Principle 
At any time: 
• One Access-Mode is primary. 
• Any other mode is secondary only. 
The primary mode: 
• defines assumptions, 
• controls conclusions, and 
• sets the level of certainty. 
Secondary modes: 
• may assist, 
• may clarify, 
• but must not decide or validate.

7. Validation and Error-Detection Discipline 
7.1 Purpose of Validation 
Validation is required because AI-assisted governance reasoning can appear coherent and 
confident even when it is incomplete, misaligned, or incorrectly inferred. 
In the Access-Mode method, validation serves three purposes: 
• to confirm that outputs are grounded in the provided materials, 
• to detect reasoning drift or mode collapse, and 
• to preserve human accountability over final interpretations. 
Validation does not assert correctness, compliance, or adequacy. 
It assesses whether the reasoning process remains within its declared posture.

7.2 Validation Is Mandatory for High-Impact Outputs 
Validation is required whenever AI-generated content is: 
• intended for external sharing, 
• used in decision support, 
• incorporated into documentation or reports, or 
• referenced in standards or regulatory contexts. 
For informal exploration, validation may be lighter. 
For high-impact or externally consumed outputs, validation is mandatory. 
Skipping validation increases the risk of: 
• silent error propagation, 
• misplaced confidence, and 
• misuse of governance artifacts.

7.3 Misalignment Testing as a Validation Method 
Misalignment testing is the primary error-detection method in the Access-Mode discipline. 
Definition

Page | 38

Misalignment testing is the deliberate modification or removal of a small number of critical 
elements in the input material in order to observe how the AI system responds. 
This method tests whether the AI output is: 
• grounded in the provided content, or 
• generated through pattern completion without sensitivity to meaning.

7.3.1 Intentional Misalignment Testing (Required Validation Step) 
For high-impact outputs, intentional misalignment testing is a required validation step prior to 
finalization. 
The test is intentionally simple and repeatable.

7.3.2 How Misalignment Testing Is Performed 
After generating an output: 
1. Remove or alter two or three critical elements, such as: 
o a definition, 
o a scope boundary, 
o a key assumption, or 
o a reference or qualifier. 
2. Re-run the same model with the altered input. 
3. Observe the response.

7.3.2 How Misalignment Testing Is Performed

7.3.3 What to Observe 
During misalignment testing, observe whether the AI system: 
• detects the inconsistency, 
• flags uncertainty or missing information, 
• propagates the error without acknowledgment, or 
• invents missing structure or justification. 
Outputs that confidently reconstruct missing meaning without evidence require human 
correction or rejection.

Page | 39

7.4 Question-Driven Verification 
Misalignment testing should be paired with direct questioning. 
Question-driven verification forces the AI system to expose: 
• assumptions, 
• inference boundaries, and 
• posture constraints. 
Examples include: 
• “Which parts of this response rely on inference rather than explicit text?” 
• “What assumptions are not directly supported by the source material?” 
• “Which Access-Mode constraints shape this answer?” 
• “What would a reviewer likely challenge here?” 
These questions should be asked before final acceptance of any output.

7.5 Mode-Aware Validation 
Validation must be aligned with the active Access-Mode. 
• ID_1 (Learning) 
Validate clarity, scope, and conceptual accuracy. 
• ID_2 (Operational) 
Validate scenario realism, uncertainty handling, and avoidance of adequacy claims. 
• ID_3 (Inspection) 
Validate language precision, traceability, and interpretability. 
Validation failure often indicates mode drift, not model malfunction.

7.6 Detecting Hallucination vs Inference 
Not all inference is error. 
The Access-Mode method distinguishes between:

• Supported inference 
Logical extension grounded in the provided material. 
• Hallucination 
Confident statements that introduce unsupported facts, obligations, or conclusions. 
Misalignment testing and question-driven verification help surface this distinction without 
requiring technical model inspection.

Validation activities should be recorded in a lightweight but consistent manner.

A session should be stopped or reset if: 
• misalignment testing repeatedly fails, 
• the AI system ignores declared mode boundaries, or 
• outputs escalate certainty without justification. 
If a different reasoning posture is required: 
• end the current session, and 
• switch to a different project with an explicit mode declaration. 
Do not force posture changes within the same session.

regardless of apparent completeness or structure.

9. Standards and Review Context 
9.1 Alignment with ISO/IEC Governance Practices 
Access-Mode aligns conceptually with established ISO/IEC governance practices that emphasize 
role separation, lifecycle awareness, interpretability, and human accountability, without 
asserting conformance to any specific standard. 
In particular, Access-Mode is compatible with governance principles commonly reflected in 
ISO/IEC work, including: 
• clear separation between learning, operation, and review activities, 
• avoidance of implicit authority or unqualified assertions, 
• preservation of human decision-making in high-impact contexts, and 
• interpretability of system behavior over time. 
Access-Mode does not implement ISO controls, requirements, or processes. 
It addresses a complementary concern: how AI systems reason when interacting with 
governance materials, regardless of which standards or frameworks are in use. 
As such, Access-Mode should be understood as supportive of good governance practice, not as 
an alternative governance standard.

9.3 How Standards Bodies and Reviewers Should Read Version E 
Standards bodies, regulators, and technical reviewers should read Version E as a reasoning 
discipline, not as a governance framework. 
When reviewing AI-assisted work that references Access-Mode: 
• Access-Mode indicates how reasoning was bounded, not whether conclusions are 
correct. 
• Mode declarations clarify intent and posture, not authority. 
• Validation practices (such as misalignment testing) indicate error-detection discipline, 
not assurance. 
Reviewers should treat Access-Mode outputs as: 
• interpretable drafts, 
• subject to challenge and human review, 
• contextual to the declared Access-Mode. 
Access-Mode is therefore best understood as a review aid, improving clarity about how AI 
assistance was used, rather than as an evaluative mechanism.

However, it may inform future work by: 
• highlighting reasoning-related failure modes in AI-assisted governance, 
• demonstrating the value of explicit posture control, 
• and providing a vocabulary for discussing cognitive boundaries in AI use. 
If normative standards addressing AI governance reasoning are developed in the future, Access-
Mode may serve as: 
• an informative reference, 
• an example of disciplined non-normative practice,

• or a source of terminology and problem framing.

10. Limitations and Explicit Non-Claims 
10.1 What Access-Mode Does Not Solve 
Access-Mode is intentionally limited in scope. 
It does not solve: 
• governance disagreements, 
• regulatory interpretation disputes, 
• organizational accountability failures, 
• or deficiencies in underlying governance artifacts. 
Access-Mode does not improve the content of governance materials. 
It improves the conditions under which AI systems reason about that content. 
If governance inputs are incomplete, ambiguous, or contested, Access-Mode will not resolve 
those issues. Instead, it is designed to make such limitations more visible, not to conceal them 
behind fluent output. 
This distinction is important. Access-Mode is not a substitute for governance maturity, 
professional judgment, or institutional responsibility.

10.2 Risks of Misapplication 
Like any method, Access-Mode can be misapplied. 
Common risks include: 
• treating Access-Mode declarations as indicators of correctness or trust, 
• assuming that disciplined reasoning implies valid conclusions, 
• or using mode labels to shield outputs from critique. 
These uses are explicitly outside the intent of this paper. 
Access-Mode does not make AI outputs right. 
It makes them easier to interpret, question, and review. 
If Access-Mode is used as a rhetorical device rather than a reasoning discipline, it loses its value. 
The method relies on good faith use by practitioners who understand that clarity is not the 
same as authority.

Page | 51

10.3 Boundaries of Automation and AI Judgment 
Access-Mode is built on a simple but firm assumption: 
Governance judgment remains a human responsibility. 
AI systems can assist with: 
• explanation, 
• exploration, 
• structuring, 
• and review preparation.

human-centred. Over-claiming capability in this space would undermine trust rather than build

for: 
• professional disagreement, 
• institutional processes,

11. Conclusion 
11.1 Reasoning Discipline as Governance Infrastructure 
This paper has argued that reasoning discipline is not a peripheral concern in AI-assisted 
governance, but a form of infrastructure in its own right. 
When AI systems are used to explain, analyze, or prepare governance materials, the way they 
reason becomes part of the governance environment — even when no execution or 
enforcement occurs. Without explicit boundaries, learning, operational analysis, and inspection 
reasoning can easily blur, creating ambiguity and misplaced confidence. 
Access-Mode is offered as a practical response to this reality. It does not introduce new 
authority or replace existing governance mechanisms. Instead, it provides a way to make 
reasoning posture visible, stable, and reviewable, so that AI assistance can be used without 
eroding accountability or interpretability. 
In this sense, reasoning discipline supports governance in the same way that clear roles, 
procedures, and documentation do: by making intent explicit and behavior understandable.

11.2 From Artifact Governance to Cognitive Governance 
Much of modern governance relies on carefully constructed artifacts — policies, standards, 
frameworks, and reports — that assume human judgment in their interpretation and use. 
As AI systems increasingly interact with these artifacts, a new layer of governance becomes 
necessary: not over the artifacts themselves, but over the cognitive processes applied to them. 
Access-Mode reflects a shift from focusing solely on what governance artifacts say, to also 
considering how reasoning about them occurs. This shift does not diminish the importance of 
artifacts. Rather, it protects their intent by ensuring that AI-assisted reasoning does not silently 
extend, reinterpret, or over-assert what those artifacts were designed to convey. 
Cognitive governance, as used here, is not a new domain of authority. It is a recognition that 
reasoning posture matters — and that preserving clarity at this level helps governance artifacts 
remain trustworthy and usable over time.

Annex C — Author’s Intent (Informative) 
This paper was developed in response to a recurring pattern observed in AI-assisted 
governance work. As AI governance progresses, a wider range of tools, roles, and expectations 
is emerging. This often increases cognitive load, specialization pressure, and management 
overhead for those responsible for learning, operating, and reviewing governance materials. 
At the same time, AI systems are becoming more sophisticated and diverse in how they reason, 
explain, and analyze. When learning, operational analysis, and inspection reasoning are 
compressed into a single interaction, outputs may sound fluent while making it harder to see 
uncertainty, intent, or responsibility clearly. 
Access-Mode is presented as a method for slowing reasoning down on purpose, not to limit 
capability, but to make complex thinking easier to follow and easier to examine. By separating 
reasoning into clear postures and keeping those postures stable, the method helps people 
understand what kind of reasoning is taking place and what it can - and cannot - support. 
The intent of this work is to support governance practice in environments where complexity is 
increasing, so that AI assistance helps explain, organize, and clarify reasoning in ways that 
strengthen clarity, accountability, and human judgment. 
Why this matters: as AI becomes more capable and more widely used in governance contexts, 
the ability to clearly understand, question, and review reasoning becomes just as important as 
the conclusions that reasoning produces. 
Thank you for taking the time to read this paper.

Edition: Companion Paper — Version E.2 
Date of Issue: 5th February 2026 
Status: Draft (Informative Companion — Non-Normative) 
Author: Anthony Siljeg 
Affiliation: Alnotrea Labs / Policy of Developments — Access PoD Initiative 
Relationship Note 
This document is an informative companion to APOD-TR-006 (Version E). It does not supersede, revise, 
or reinterpret the Access-Mode method. 
Intended Audience 
Standards bodies, reviewers, governance practitioners, facilitators, and contributors publishing or 
inspecting Working-PoD artifacts.

Abstract 
Version E.2 complements the Access-Mode method by explaining the lifecycle of governance 
artifacts as they move from exploratory drafts to inspection-ready Working-PoDs. 
This paper does not restate the Access-Mode method, redeﬁne reasoning postures, or 
introduce new governance requirements. Instead, it clariﬁes how the canonical six-module 
structure may be populated under diﬀerent Access-Modes, how the meaning of “ﬁlled” changes 
by posture, and under what conditions a Working-PoD may be considered frozen for inspection. 
Version E.2 also deﬁnes how complete Working-PoD examples should be read and interpreted 
when published separately for learning, operational reasoning, or inspection illustration. These 
examples are informative only and do not assert correctness, compliance, or readiness. 
This document is methodological and non-normative. It is intended to support standards 
exploration, reviewer interpretation, and disciplined governance practice by making artifact 
state, posture, and inspection boundaries explicit.

1. Introduction 
1.1 Purpose of Version E.2 
Version E.2 is an informative companion to the Access-Mode method defined in Version E. Its 
purpose is to clarify how governance artifacts move through different stages of completeness 
and interpretation as they are reasoned about under different Access-Modes, and how those 
artifacts become inspection-ready Working-PoDs. 
Version E established Access-Mode as a reasoning orchestration method, explicitly separating 
learning, operational, and inspection reasoning postures. While that paper defines how 
reasoning is controlled, it intentionally avoids prescribing how governance artifacts should be 
assembled, frozen, or published across different contexts. 
Version E.2 addresses this remaining source of ambiguity by explaining: 
• how the canonical six-module structure may be populated under different reasoning 
postures, 
• how the meaning of “filled” changes by Access-Mode, 
• how and when a Working-PoD may be considered frozen for inspection, and 
• how complete Working-PoD examples should be interpreted when published separately 
for learning or illustration. 
This paper does not restate the Access-Mode method, redefine reasoning postures, introduce 
governance requirements, or assert compliance, readiness, or correctness. It exists to make the 
artifact lifecycle explicit without altering the method that governs reasoning about those 
artifacts.

1.2 Relationship to Version E (Access-Mode Method) 
Version E remains the canonical reference for the Access-Mode method. All definitions of 
reasoning posture, mode discipline, validation, and non-normative status are inherited 
unchanged. 
Version E.2 is subordinate and complementary. It assumes that: 
• Access-Mode governs how reasoning occurs, 
• Working-PoDs govern what exists at a point in time, and 
• reasoning posture and artifact state must remain explicitly distinct. 
Where Version E answers the question “What kind of reasoning is permitted here?”, Version E.2 
answers the question “What does this artifact represent at this stage?”

Page | 4

1.2 Relationship to Version E (Access-Mode Method) 
Version E remains the canonical reference for the Access-Mode method. All definitions of 
reasoning posture, mode discipline, validation, and non-normative status are inherited 
unchanged. 
Version E.2 is subordinate and complementary. It assumes that: 
• Access-Mode governs how reasoning occurs, 
• Working-PoDs govern what exists at a point in time, and 
• reasoning posture and artifact state must remain explicitly distinct. 
Where Version E answers the question “What kind of reasoning is permitted here?”, Version E.2 
answers the question “What does this artifact represent at this stage?”

Page | 4

Nothing in Version E.2 alters the meaning of ID_1, ID_2, or ID_3 as defined in Version E. Where 
ambiguity arises, Version E prevails.

2. Reasoning Posture vs Artifact State 
2.1 Access-Mode as Reasoning Posture Control 
Access-Mode defines reasoning posture as a project-level control over how AI-assisted 
reasoning is conducted when working with governance materials. Each Access-Mode 
constrains: 
• what assumptions may be made, 
• what level of certainty may be expressed, and 
• what kinds of conclusions are permitted. 
As established in Version E: 
• ID_1 governs learning and conceptual understanding, 
• ID_2 governs exploratory and uncertainty-aware operational reasoning, and 
• ID_3 governs inspection-oriented review and interpretation. 
These modes are non-equivalent and non-progressive. They do not represent stages of maturity 
or approval. They represent distinct cognitive postures applied to the same underlying 
materials. 
Access-Mode therefore governs interpretation and reasoning behavior, not artifact 
completeness, correctness, or readiness.

2.2 Working-PoDs as Stateful Artifact Snapshots 
A Working-PoD is a stateful snapshot of governance artifacts assembled using the canonical six-
module structure defined in earlier workshop and artifact releases. A Working-PoD captures 
what exists at a specific moment, not how that content should be reasoned about.

Page | 5

excerpt:
2.2 Working-PoDs as Stateful Artifact Snapshots 
A Working-PoD is a stateful snapshot of governance artifacts assembled using the canonical six-
module structure defined in earlier workshop and artifact releases. A Working-PoD captures 
what exists at a specific moment, not how that content should be reasoned about.

Page | 5

The same six-module structure may be populated under different Access-Modes without 
structural change. What differs is not the schema, but the meaning of population under each 
posture. 
Under this model: 
• A Working-PoD populated under ID_1 represents conceptual understanding, learning 
progress, or platform development exploration. 
• A Working-PoD populated under ID_2 represents scenario-based reasoning, stress-
testing, and operational uncertainty exploration. 
• A Working-PoD populated under ID_3 represents material prepared for inspection, 
where traceability, enumeration, and explicit gaps are required. 
Importantly, artifact state does not imply reasoning posture, and reasoning posture does not 
imply artifact readiness. A complete-looking artifact populated under ID_1 or ID_2 does not 
become inspection-ready by appearance alone. 
A Working-PoD becomes inspection-ready only when: 
• artifacts are explicitly frozen, 
• the governing posture is ID_3, 
• and inspection constraints defined in Version E are applied. 
This separation ensures that learning, operational exploration, and inspection preparation can 
reuse the same structure without collapsing authority, certainty, or interpretive boundaries.

2.3 Why the Distinction Matters 
Without explicit separation between reasoning posture and artifact state, governance work 
risks subtle but consequential misinterpretation: 
• Learning artifacts may be mistaken for review conclusions. 
• Operational scenarios may be misread as adequacy claims. 
• Inspection-oriented clarity may be mistaken for endorsement. 
By distinguishing how reasoning is constrained from what artifact state exists, Version E.2 
preserves the intent of Access-Mode while enabling complete, teachable examples to be 
published without inflating their authority.

3. The Working-PoD Lifecycle 
3.1 Overview of Lifecycle States 
A Working-PoD progresses through a small number of explicit lifecycle states that describe 
artifact condition, not governance quality or outcome. These states exist to make it clear what 
a set of artifacts represents at a given moment, and how it may be used without 
misinterpretation. 
The lifecycle described here is descriptive, not prescriptive. It does not mandate progression, 
sequence, or completion. Artifacts may remain indefinitely in any state, or move backward, 
without implying deficiency or failure. 
The lifecycle exists to support interpretability, review discipline, and controlled publication — 
not maturity scoring or readiness assessment.

3.2 Draft State 
The draft state represents governance artifacts that are being explored, clarified, or developed 
without any expectation of completeness, stability, or external review. 
Draft Working-PoDs commonly arise under ID_1 (learning) or early ID_2 (operational 
reasoning) postures. 
In this state: 
• modules may be partially populated, 
• content may be reflective, provisional, or exploratory, 
• assumptions may be incomplete or evolving, 
• internal inconsistencies may exist by design. 
Draft artifacts are non-inspectable by definition. 
They are not intended to withstand external scrutiny, nor to be interpreted as coherent 
positions. 
The draft state is essential. It preserves space for learning, uncertainty, and conceptual 
development without prematurely signaling authority or intent.

The draft state represents governance artifacts that are being explored, clarified, or developed

Draft Working-PoDs commonly arise under ID_1 (learning) or early ID_2 (operational

The draft state is essential. It preserves space for learning, uncertainty, and conceptual

Page | 7

3.3 Populated (Posture-Bound) State 
A Working-PoD enters a populated state when all modules in the canonical structure are filled 
according to the constraints of a declared Access-Mode. 
Population does not mean finality. It means that, within a given posture, the artifact set is 
internally complete enough to support reasoning under that posture. 
Population is therefore posture-bound: 
• Under ID_1, population reflects conceptual coverage and learning completeness. 
• Under ID_2, population reflects scenario coverage, stress exploration, and uncertainty 
articulation. 
• Under ID_3, population reflects enumerated content prepared for inspection. 
A populated Working-PoD may look structurally complete across modes while representing 
very different kinds of content and intent. 
Critically, population alone does not confer inspectability. 
A populated Working-PoD remains non-inspectable unless it is explicitly frozen under ID_3.

3.4 Frozen State (Inspection-Ready) 
A Working-PoD enters a frozen state only when it is intentionally prepared for inspection under 
ID_3 reasoning posture. 
Freezing is a deliberate act, not an emergent condition. It signals that: 
• the artifact set is no longer exploratory, 
• content is intended to be read as issued, 
• and interpretation risk must be controlled. 
When frozen: 
• modules are enumerated and internally consistent, 
• scope and exclusions are explicit, 
• known gaps are recorded rather than inferred away, 
• and traceability expectations are met. 
Freezing does not imply: 
• correctness,

• approval,

It indicates only that the artifact set is stable enough to be inspected as a snapshot, challenged
