3.5 Transitions Between States 
Transitions between lifecycle states are contextual and human-controlled. 
There is no requirement that artifacts move linearly from draft to populated to frozen. Artifacts 
may: 
• remain populated but unfrozen, 
• revert from frozen to populated if scope changes, 
• or be abandoned without ever reaching inspection readiness. 
What matters is not progression, but explicit signaling. 
Each transition should be accompanied by: 
• an explicit Access-Mode declaration, 
• a clear statement of intended use, 
• and, where applicable, a statement of limitations. 
Silent transitions — especially from populated to frozen — are a primary source of governance 
risk and must be avoided.

3.6 Lifecycle States and Governance Risk 
The Working-PoD lifecycle exists to prevent a common failure pattern in AI-assisted 
governance: confusing completeness with authority. 
Without explicit lifecycle signaling: 
• learning artifacts may be reused as operational guidance, 
• operational scenarios may be treated as inspection conclusions, 
• inspection-ready artifacts may be mistaken for approval signals.

Page | 9

By making lifecycle state explicit, the Access-Mode method and the Working-PoD construct 
work together to ensure that artifact condition, reasoning posture, and interpretive authority 
remain distinct. 
This separation is foundational to disciplined governance practice in environments where AI 
systems are used to assist reasoning, drafting, and review.

This separation is foundational to disciplined governance practice in environments where AI

4. Freeze Conditions for Inspection 
4.1 Inspection as a Distinct and Exclusive Posture 
Inspection is a distinct governance activity with its own risks and interpretive pressures. For this 
reason, a Working-PoD may be considered inspection-ready only when governed by ID_3 — 
Inspection and Review reasoning posture, as defined in Version E. 
No other Access-Mode permits freezing. 
• ID_1 prioritizes understanding and conceptual exploration. 
• ID_2 prioritizes scenario-based reasoning and uncertainty exploration. 
• ID_3 prioritizes clarity, traceability, and external interpretability. 
These postures are intentionally non-equivalent. Treating learning or operational reasoning as a 
basis for inspection introduces ambiguity and risks misrepresenting intent. 
Inspection readiness is therefore not a matter of artifact maturity, but of posture discipline.

4.2 Explicit Freeze Declaration 
Freezing a Working-PoD is a conscious and documented act. It must be explicit. 
A Working-PoD is considered frozen for inspection only when: 
• ID_3 is declared as the governing Access-Mode, 
• the artifact set is treated as issued for review, 
• and further modification is suspended or versioned.

Page | 10

Implicit freezing — where artifacts are reused, shared, or cited as if stable without declaration 
— is not permitted under this method. 
An explicit freeze declaration ensures that reviewers understand: 
• what is being inspected, 
• under what posture it was prepared, 
• and what interpretive boundaries apply.

For this reason, a Working-PoD may be considered inspection-ready only when governed by ID_3 — Inspection and Review reasoning posture, as defined in Version E.
4.2 Explicit Freeze Declaration Freezing a Working-PoD is a conscious and documented act.

A Working-PoD is considered frozen for inspection only when: • ID_3 is declared as the governing Access-Mode, • the artifact set is treated as issued for review, • and further modification is suspended or versioned.
An explicit freeze declaration ensures that reviewers understand: • what is being inspected, • under what posture it was prepared, • and what interpretive boundaries apply.

excerpt:
Implicit freezing — where artifacts are reused, shared, or cited as if stable without declaration 
— is not permitted under this method. 
An explicit freeze declaration ensures that reviewers understand: 
• what is being inspected, 
• under what posture it was prepared, 
• and what interpretive boundaries apply.

4.3 Minimum Conditions for an Inspection Freeze 
To be frozen under ID_3, a Working-PoD must satisfy a minimum set of structural conditions. 
These conditions do not assert quality or adequacy. They exist to support inspectability. 
At minimum: 
• All six modules are present and populated in a manner consistent with ID_3 posture. 
• Scope, exclusions, and assumptions are explicitly stated. 
• Claims, if any, are traceable to referenced material or are clearly framed as 
observations. 
• Known gaps, limitations, or unresolved issues are recorded rather than inferred away. 
Completeness here refers to enumeration and clarity, not sufficiency or correctness.

4.4 Traceability and Stability Expectations 
Inspection depends on the ability to trace content without reconstructing intent. 
Accordingly, a frozen Working-PoD must exhibit: 
• stable identifiers or version references, 
• consistent internal structure, 
• and resistance to silent change. 
Traceability does not require exhaustive logging or technical instrumentation. It requires that a 
reviewer can understand: 
• what content was included, 
• what content was excluded, 
• and what has changed since the prior state.

Page | 11

If traceability cannot be maintained, the Working-PoD should not be frozen.

4.5 Recording Gaps and Uncertainty 
Inspection-ready does not mean complete. 
A critical condition of freezing under ID_3 is the explicit recording of gaps, uncertainty, and 
limitation. 
Silence is not neutral. 
Unstated gaps are routinely misinterpreted as resolved issues. 
Under ID_3: 
• uncertainty must be surfaced, not smoothed, 
• gaps must be recorded, not compensated for, 
• and absence of evidence must be stated explicitly. 
This discipline protects both reviewers and authors by preventing fluent language from masking 
unresolved issues.

4.6 What Freezing Does Not Mean 
To avoid misinterpretation, freezing a Working-PoD does not imply: 
• that the artifacts are correct, 
• that governance controls are adequate, 
• that compliance has been achieved, 
• that approval has been granted, 
• or that deployment is appropriate. 
Freezing indicates only that the artifact set is stable enough to be inspected as issued, and that 
its posture and limitations are explicit. 
Inspection improves interpretability. 
It does not grant authority.

4.7 Reopening or Revising a Frozen Working-PoD

Page | 12

A frozen Working-PoD may be reopened if: 
• scope changes, 
• assumptions are invalidated, 
• or new information materially alters interpretation. 
Reopening must be explicit. The artifact set should return to a populated or draft state under 
an appropriate Access-Mode before being refrozen. 
Silent modification of a frozen Working-PoD undermines inspectability and should be treated as 
a governance failure.

5. Interpreting Working-PoD Examples 
5.1 Purpose of Published Working-PoD Examples 
Working-PoD examples may be published as informative companion artifacts to support 
learning, discussion, and disciplined governance practice. Their purpose is illustrative rather 
than authoritative. 
Examples are intended to show how the same canonical six-module structure can be 
populated under different Access-Modes without changing schema, semantics, or method 
boundaries. They demonstrate posture-dependent interpretation, not preferred content or 
outcomes. 
Published examples do not define requirements, prescribe implementation, or establish 
benchmarks. They exist to make abstract distinctions concrete while preserving the non-
normative status of the Access-Mode method.

5.2 General Rules for Reading Examples

Page | 13

All Working-PoD examples must be read in the context of their explicitly declared Access-
Mode. 
Readers should assume that: 
• the example reflects only the reasoning posture under which it was created, 
• content is illustrative of posture, not exhaustive of governance practice, 
• and omissions or gaps may be intentional. 
Examples should never be treated as: 
• reference implementations, 
• baseline expectations, 
• maturity indicators, 
• or templates for compliance. 
If an example appears to suggest authority, sufficiency, or readiness, it is being misread.

5.3 Learning Examples (ID_1) 
Working-PoD examples published under ID_1 (learning posture) are conceptual by design. 
Their purpose is to: 
• demonstrate governance reasoning foundations, 
• explore scope, intent, and assumptions, 
• and support platform or practitioner learning. 
ID_1 examples may include: 
• provisional language, 
• reflective answers, 
• incomplete references, 
• and unresolved questions. 
These examples are explicitly non-inspectable. 
They do not aim for traceability, enumeration, or external defensibility. 
Completeness in an ID_1 example means conceptual coverage, not rigor or stability.

Page | 14

5.4 Operational Examples (ID_2) 
Working-PoD examples published under ID_2 (operational reasoning posture) are scenario-
oriented and uncertainty-aware. 
Their purpose is to: 
• explore how governance concepts behave under stress, 
• surface failure modes and fragility, 
• and examine hypothetical runtime conditions. 
ID_2 examples may include: 
• conditional reasoning, 
• speculative scenarios, 
• conflicting signals, 
• and intentionally unresolved outcomes. 
These examples are not inspection-ready, regardless of apparent detail or structure. 
They are not intended to demonstrate adequacy, effectiveness, or correctness. 
Completeness in an ID_2 example means coverage of scenarios and uncertainty, not resolution.

Working-PoD examples published under ID_3 (inspection posture) are prepared as frozen 
artifact snapshots. 
Their purpose is to: 
• illustrate inspection discipline, 
• demonstrate traceability and explicit limitation handling, 
• and support reviewer interpretation and challenge. 
ID_3 examples are: 
• enumerated, 
• stable as issued, 
• and explicit about scope, assumptions, and gaps. 
Even so, ID_3 examples remain non-authoritative. 
They are challengeable artifacts, not validated outcomes.

The following misinterpretations are common and must be avoided when reading Working-PoD

• Treating ID_1 or ID_2 examples as precursors to inspection readiness.

• Treating ID_3 examples as endorsements or adequacy signals.

Each example exists within its declared posture only. 
Cross-posture comparison without context introduces governance risk.

Title: Governed Dataset Onboarding and Lifecycle Routing for AI Training Systems 
Dataset Passport and State-Based Lifecycle Framework 
Edition: First Edition 
Date of Issue: 10th March 2026 
Status: Public Review Draft (Standards Exploration) 
Author: Anthony Siljeg 
Affiliation: Alnotrea Labs / Policy of Developments - Access PoD Initiative.

Document Scope 
This technical report deﬁnes a governance framework for dataset onboarding, lifecycle routing, and 
dataset passport metadata used in AI training environments. 
The report establishes governance semantics and lifecycle principles but does not prescribe a 
speciﬁc machine learning architecture, training pipeline, or execution environment. 
Execution systems such as Q-Pathformer or other training architectures may consume lifecycle-
governed datasets produced under this framework, but such systems do not deﬁne governance 
authority within the Access-PoD model.

This document extends the governance framework established in APOD-TR-002 (Version A), the 
architecture illustration described in APOD-TR-003 (Version B), and the onboarding discipline deﬁned in 
APOD-TR-004 (Version C). It introduces a dataset lifecycle and passport model designed to enable 
governed transformation of inspection artifacts and other structured records into machine-readable 
datasets for AI training environments.

Abstract 
Artificial intelligence systems require large volumes of training data, yet the sources of that 
data increasingly originate from governance artifacts, inspection records, simulation outputs, 
and operational knowledge rather than conventional datasets. Converting these materials into 
machine-readable training inputs introduces a governance challenge: provenance, 
authorization scope, and lifecycle constraints must be preserved while enabling controlled use 
in model development.

Page | 2

This paper introduces a governed dataset onboarding framework designed to bridge that gap. 
The framework defines how inspection-grade artifacts and other governed data sources can be 
transformed into structured datasets while maintaining lineage, authorization boundaries, and 
containment controls. Central to the approach is the Dataset Passport, a machine-readable 
declaration that records provenance, authorized use, and routing constraints for each dataset 
unit. 
The model also introduces a multi-state dataset lifecycle in which datasets transition through 
controlled stages of evaluation, runtime use, and durable training eligibility. This lifecycle 
prevents uncontrolled dataset mutation and ensures that promotion into persistent training 
corpora occurs only through explicit governance review. 
The framework operates under the governance principles defined in Access-PoD Version B and 
Version C. It does not confer dataset certification, compliance approval, or trust designation. 
Instead, it provides a structured mechanism for traceability, containment, and controlled 
dataset evolution. While compatible with a variety of AI training environments, the framework 
may optionally interoperate with execution systems such as Q-Pathformer or other machine 
learning architectures capable of consuming lifecycle-governed datasets. 
By separating governance authority from training execution, the model enables organizations 
to transform governed artifacts into usable AI datasets without sacrificing transparency, 
auditability, or operational control.

applying similar principles to datasets themselves. Datasets entering AI training environments 
may also originate under uncertain conditions, particularly when derived from inspection

Relationship to the Q-Pathformer Multi-State Training Concept 
The three-state dataset lifecycle model described in this document is conceptually aligned with 
earlier work describing multi-state machine learning architectures. 
The original architectural concept was introduced in December 2024 in the publication 
Q-Pathformer: Multi-state Machine Learning and LLM Training, which describes a training 
architecture operating across three interacting states for pre-training, vector convergence, and 
fine-tuning processes. 
Reference document: QPATH-ARCH-001 
(Q-Pathformer: Multi-state Machine Learning Architecture) 
In that architecture, data flows dynamically across three processing states that organize 
exploratory signals, trained vector relationships, and finalized training outputs. 
The lifecycle model defined in this report applies a similar three-state separation to dataset 
governance rather than model execution. The purpose is to preserve containment and 
traceability as datasets evolve from provisional runtime signals to durable training corpora. 
Within the Access-PoD research series, governance authority remains defined by the Access-
PoD framework publications (Version A through Version C and subsequent reports). Execution 
architectures such as Q-Pathformer are treated as optional implementation environments that 
may consume lifecycle-governed datasets but do not determine governance authority.

extensive collections of documents, analytical records, and simulation outputs that contain 
structured insights relevant to machine learning. 
Examples include policy analysis reports, governance inspection records, engineering design 
reviews, operational simulations, and compliance documentation. While these artifacts often 
contain valuable information, they are rarely structured in a format suitable for direct use in AI 
training pipelines. 
Attempting to convert such artifacts directly into datasets can introduce several governance 
risks. 
First, the provenance of individual dataset elements may become unclear. Without explicit 
lineage tracking, it becomes difficult to determine the origin of training signals or to verify 
whether the data was collected under appropriate authorization conditions. 
Second, the intended use of the data may be exceeded. Artifacts created for analytical or 
governance purposes may contain context-specific reasoning that should not automatically 
become part of a durable model training corpus. 
Third, datasets derived from evolving operational environments may change over time. 
Without versioned lifecycle management, training datasets may be overwritten or mutated in 
ways that obscure the historical record of how models were developed. 
These challenges highlight the need for a structured mechanism that preserves provenance and 
authorization constraints while enabling controlled dataset transformation. 
The framework proposed in this paper addresses these challenges through three mechanisms: 
1. Dataset Passports, which declare provenance and authorization scope for each dataset 
unit. 
2. State-based dataset routing, which separates provisional runtime datasets from 
durable training datasets. 
3. Controlled promotion rules, which require governance review before datasets enter 
persistent training corpora. 
Together, these mechanisms create a governance-aligned bridge between inspection artifacts 
and machine-readable training datasets.

enter the lifecycle through a dataset onboarding stage in which artifacts are ingested, 
converted into machine-readable structures, and assigned Dataset Passports. Routing decisions 
are then applied according to provenance, authorization scope, and containment constraints. 
Datasets are subsequently managed across three lifecycle states: State 3 for runtime and

Each state represents a different stage of dataset maturity and authorization.

4.1 State 3 — Runtime and Synthetic Dataset Layer 
State 3 is the default entry point for newly onboarded datasets. Datasets routed to this state 
are considered provisional or contextual resources that may be used for runtime reasoning, 
simulation, or synthetic dataset generation. 
State 3 datasets commonly originate from sources such as: 
• inspection artifacts produced under governance workflows 
• simulation records or scenario analyses 
• operational logs and analytical outputs 
• newly ingested external datasets awaiting evaluation 
Because these datasets may contain contextual reasoning signals rather than validated training 
knowledge, they are treated as temporary or exploratory inputs rather than permanent 
training material. 
Typical uses of State 3 datasets include: 
• runtime reasoning support 
• synthetic dataset generation 
• contextual memory structures 
• experimental training signals 
State 3 datasets remain traceable through dataset passports and lineage records, ensuring that 
their origin and authorization scope remain visible even during experimental use.

4.2 State 2 — Transition and Validation Layer

4.2 State 2 — Transition and Validation Layer

Page | 12

State 2 acts as a precautionary transition layer between provisional datasets and durable 
training datasets. 
The purpose of State 2 is to verify that datasets satisfy governance requirements before they 
become part of a persistent training corpus. This stage introduces structured validation 
processes that examine dataset provenance, authorization status, and lifecycle constraints. 
Typical State 2 validation activities include: 
• verifying dataset lineage records 
• confirming authorization scope and ownership 
• evaluating dataset quality and relevance 
• assessing governance constraints and disclosure limits 
• ensuring compatibility with organizational policies 
Datasets may remain in State 2 for extended periods if governance review or additional 
validation is required. The transition layer therefore acts as a containment mechanism that 
prevents premature integration of datasets into model training.

5. Dataset Passport Model 
The dataset lifecycle model introduced in the previous section requires a structured mechanism 
for recording dataset provenance, authorization scope, and lifecycle status. To support this 
requirement, the framework introduces the Dataset Passport, a machine-readable record that 
accompanies each dataset unit entering the onboarding pipeline. 
The Dataset Passport acts as a governance-aligned declaration of dataset identity and 
permitted usage. It records the origin of the dataset, the lifecycle state in which the dataset 
currently resides, and the authorization conditions under which the dataset may be used. 
Importantly, the Dataset Passport does not function as a certification mechanism. It does not 
grant approval, trust designation, compliance status, or assurance claims. Instead, it provides 
traceability and operational guidance for dataset routing within the lifecycle model. 
Dataset passports are therefore informative governance artifacts, not authoritative 
determinations.

5.1 Purpose of the Dataset Passport 
The Dataset Passport fulfills several roles within the dataset onboarding framework. 
First, it preserves dataset provenance. Each passport records the origin of the dataset artifact 
and references the canonical records from which the dataset was derived. This ensures that 
lineage information remains visible even when datasets are transformed into machine-readable 
structures. 
Second, the passport defines authorization scope. Organizations may permit datasets to be 
used for specific purposes such as runtime reasoning, synthetic dataset generation, or model 
fine-tuning. These permissions are recorded within the passport so that dataset routing 
mechanisms can enforce the intended usage boundaries. 
Third, the passport records dataset lifecycle status. The passport identifies whether a dataset 
currently resides in State 3, State 2, or State 1. This allows training pipelines to treat datasets 
differently depending on their maturity and authorization level.

The Dataset Passport provides the governance metadata required to manage datasets 
throughout the lifecycle. 
The passport records the dataset’s identity, provenance anchors, lifecycle state, and 
authorization scope. Lineage references preserve traceability between dataset versions and the 
artifacts from which they were derived. 
Optional execution metadata may be included when datasets are consumed by training 
environments such as Q-Pathformer. However, execution metadata does not alter governance 
authority or lifecycle status. 
The passport therefore acts as a governance boundary, ensuring that datasets remain 
traceable and policy-constrained even when used within model training pipelines. 
A Dataset Passport contains several categories of information. 
These categories are designed to support both governance oversight and automated dataset 
routing. 
Typical fields include: 
• dataset identity 
• provenance anchors 
• lifecycle state 
• authorization scope 
• lineage references 
• optional execution metadata

5.3 Provenance Anchors 
Provenance anchors provide cryptographic and documentary references to the artifacts from 
which the dataset was derived. 
In the case of datasets originating from Access-PoD inspection workflows, provenance anchors 
typically reference ID_3 frozen artifacts and their associated hash manifests. These anchors 
ensure that dataset lineage remains verifiable even after artifacts are transformed into 
machine-readable structures.

Typical provenance anchors may include: 
• source artifact identifiers 
• canonical artifact filenames 
• cryptographic hashes of frozen artifacts 
• freeze timestamps 
• governance mode identifiers 
Together, these anchors allow auditors or governance authorities to trace a dataset back to its 
original inspection records.

5.4 Authorization Scope 
The authorization section of the Dataset Passport defines the permitted uses of the dataset. 
Authorization scopes may vary depending on organizational policies, regulatory requirements, 
or contractual obligations. The passport records these permissions so that dataset routing 
systems can enforce them automatically.

• synthetic dataset generation 
• model fine-tuning 
• external model training 
• research experimentation

change or if dataset conditions evolve, new passport versions can update the authorization 
scope while preserving the historical record.

5.6 Lineage References 
Datasets often evolve through multiple transformation stages. For example, a dataset derived 
from inspection artifacts may later be refined into a curated training corpus. 
To preserve traceability, the Dataset Passport includes lineage references that link related 
dataset versions. 
Lineage records may reference: 
• parent dataset passports 
• earlier dataset versions 
• policy lineage records 
• source artifact identifiers 
These references ensure that dataset evolution remains visible and reversible. 
Lineage records are informative documentation, not indicators of approval or trust status. 
Their purpose is to support traceability and governance oversight.

architectures. However, execution environments may require additional metadata to organize 
datasets during training.

5.A - Dataset Containment Principle 
The dataset onboarding framework operates under a foundational constraint referred to as the 
Dataset Containment Principle. 
This principle ensures that datasets entering AI training environments remain subject to 
governance constraints throughout their lifecycle and cannot implicitly acquire authority, trust 
status, or operational approval merely by existing within a dataset pipeline. 
Dataset containment applies to all lifecycle states and all dataset transformation processes. 
Under this principle, the presence of a dataset within the onboarding framework does not 
imply: 
• dataset approval 
• dataset certification 
• dataset trustworthiness 
• model safety 
• compliance determination 
• regulatory acceptance 
Datasets are treated as evidence-bearing artifacts, not authoritative knowledge sources.

records, or analytical outputs remain context-bound and subject to explicit authorization 
controls before influencing durable model behavior.

6. Dataset Authorization and Routing 
The dataset onboarding framework requires a structured mechanism for determining how 
datasets are used once they enter the lifecycle pipeline. Dataset authorization and routing 
define the operational logic that determines whether a dataset may be used for runtime 
reasoning, synthetic dataset generation, or durable model training. 
Authorization decisions are not determined solely by dataset origin. Instead, routing decisions 
are derived from a combination of factors recorded within the Dataset Passport, including 
provenance anchors, lifecycle state, authorization scope, and governance constraints. 
Dataset routing therefore acts as the operational layer that translates governance declarations 
into dataset behavior within AI training environments.

Datasets entering the onboarding pipeline follow default routing rules designed to preserve

6.4 State 2 Signal Convergence 
Within the dataset lifecycle model, State 2 functions as the convergence layer for teacher and 
student signals. 
Teacher signals originate from structured dataset artifacts such as inspection records, scenario 
analyses, governance annotations, or curated prompts. These signals represent structured 
reasoning inputs contained within the dataset. 
Student signals represent the interpretive learning processes that attempt to extract patterns 
or insights from those signals during dataset evaluation or training preparation. 
In State 2, these signals are examined together to determine whether the dataset 
demonstrates sufficient coherence and contextual clarity to support further lifecycle 
progression. 
This convergence does not produce authoritative decisions by itself. Instead, it supports the 
validation processes that inform dataset promotion or continued containment. 
Examples of convergence evaluation activities may include: 
• assessing whether teacher signals provide consistent reasoning pathways 
• examining how student interpretations respond to those signals 
• identifying contradictions or uncertainty within the dataset signals 
• evaluating whether the dataset supports stable learning patterns 
By examining both signal types together, the State 2 layer reinforces the interpretive discipline 
introduced in Section 4. Rather than treating datasets as static knowledge sources, the system 
evaluates how reasoning signals interact before allowing them to influence durable model 
behavior.

7.1 Purpose of Dataset Lineage 
The primary purpose of dataset lineage is to preserve traceable continuity between dataset 
artifacts and the processes that created or modified them. 
AI training datasets often undergo multiple transformations. Raw artifacts may be converted 
into machine-readable records, refined through validation processes, and eventually 
incorporated into curated training corpora. Without lineage tracking, it becomes difficult to 
determine how training signals entered a model or how dataset versions relate to earlier 
artifacts. 
Dataset lineage addresses this challenge by recording: 
• the origin of dataset artifacts 
• the transformation processes applied to those artifacts 
• the relationships between dataset versions 
• the governance context associated with each dataset stage 
These records allow organizations to reconstruct dataset evolution and verify that dataset 
transformations occurred under appropriate governance conditions.

7.2 Informative Nature of Lineage Records 
Lineage records are informative documentation, not indicators of dataset validity or trust 
status. 
Recording the lineage of a dataset does not imply that the dataset has been approved for 
model training, that the dataset is free from bias or error, or that the dataset meets any 
regulatory compliance standard. 
Instead, lineage records provide contextual information that allows governance authorities and 
auditors to understand how datasets were created and how they changed over time. 
This distinction is important for maintaining the governance boundaries established in earlier 
publications. Dataset presence within lineage records must not be interpreted as evidence of 
operational readiness, certification, or assurance.

7.4 Dataset Versioning 
Datasets evolve over time as they move through the lifecycle states defined earlier in this 
document. For example, a dataset initially used for runtime reasoning may later be refined into 
a curated training dataset.

than in-place modification. 
When a dataset changes in ways that affect its content, authorization scope, or lifecycle status, 
a new dataset passport version should be issued. The new passport references the previous 
version through lineage records, creating a chain of dataset evolution. 
Versioned dataset updates allow organizations to maintain historical visibility into how training

8. Controlled Dataset Promotion 
The dataset lifecycle model introduced in earlier sections separates provisional datasets from 
durable training datasets. To preserve governance control, transitions between lifecycle states 
must occur through structured promotion events. 
Dataset promotion refers to the process by which a dataset moves from a provisional or 
exploratory lifecycle state into a durable training dataset authorized for persistent use. 
Promotion events ensure that datasets influencing long-term model behavior are introduced in 
a controlled and traceable manner.

8.1 Promotion Principles 
Dataset promotion operates under several guiding principles. 
First, promotion must be explicit and versioned. A dataset does not become a durable training 
dataset simply by existing within a dataset pipeline. Promotion requires the issuance of a new 
dataset passport version that records the lifecycle transition. 
Second, promotion must remain traceable through lineage records. The newly promoted 
dataset must reference its parent dataset and the artifacts from which it was derived. 
Third, promotion must preserve dataset containment. If portions of a dataset exceed their 
authorization scope or governance boundaries, those portions must be removed or filtered 
before the dataset becomes eligible for durable training. 
These principles ensure that dataset promotion remains transparent and reversible.

Dataset promotion operates under several guiding principles. 
First, promotion must be explicit and versioned. A dataset does not become a durable training 
dataset simply by existing within a dataset pipeline. Promotion requires the issuance of a new 
dataset passport version that records the lifecycle transition. 
Second, promotion must remain traceable through lineage records. The newly promoted 
dataset must reference its parent dataset and the artifacts from which it was derived. 
Third, promotion must preserve dataset containment. If portions of a dataset exceed their 
authorization scope or governance boundaries, those portions must be removed or filtered 
before the dataset becomes eligible for durable training. 
These principles ensure that dataset promotion remains transparent and reversible.

8.2 Promotion from State 3 to State 1 
Datasets initially routed to State 3 are considered provisional resources that may support 
runtime reasoning, simulation, or synthetic dataset generation. While these datasets may 
contain valuable signals, they are not automatically eligible for inclusion in durable training 
corpora. 
Promotion from State 3 to State 1 occurs only after governance validation confirms that the 
dataset meets the requirements for persistent training use. 
Typical promotion steps may include: 
1. verifying dataset provenance and lineage anchors 
2. evaluating the coherence of teacher and student signals 
3. confirming the dataset’s authorization scope 
4. filtering dataset elements that exceed their permitted usage 
5. issuing a new dataset passport reflecting the State 1 lifecycle status 
Once these steps are completed, the dataset may be introduced into durable training pipelines.

9. Optional Execution Environments 
The dataset onboarding framework described in this document is designed to operate 
independently of any single model architecture, training substrate, or execution environment. 
Its primary purpose is to preserve governance context, dataset provenance, lifecycle state, and 
authorization constraints as datasets move from governed artifacts into machine-readable 
forms. 
For this reason, the framework is execution-agnostic by design. A dataset may be onboarded, 
assigned a Dataset Passport, and routed through lifecycle states without requiring a specific 
training implementation. This preserves the separation established in earlier Access-PoD 
publications between governance authority and execution mechanisms. Version B explicitly 
treats architecture-specific implementations as illustrative and non-authoritative, while Version 
C preserves containment and controlled onboarding as the governing posture for operational 
transition. 
APOD-TR-004_Vol2_Version-C 
At the same time, many organizations will require an execution environment capable of 
consuming routed datasets, organizing them into training-ready structures, and preserving 
provenance during training or runtime use. For such cases, the onboarding framework may 
interoperate with optional execution environments through extension metadata recorded in 
the Dataset Passport.

The governance model defined in this document does not depend on a particular machine 
learning platform. Its core components remain the same regardless of the downstream 
execution environment: 
• Dataset Passports 
• lifecycle state declarations

9.2 Q-Pathformer as a Compatible Reference Environment 
One compatible execution environment for this framework is Q-Pathformer, which may serve 
as an optional reference substrate for governed dataset transformation, clustering, and staged 
training preparation. 
Q-Pathformer is described as a dataset training platform built around reproducibility, audit-
grade provenance, modular capsule packaging, and structured dataset curation. Its architecture 
emphasizes versioned and validated training units, making it compatible with the governance 
requirements of dataset passports and lifecycle routing. 
The Q-Pathformer materials also describe a hybrid architecture in which Access-PoD acts as the 
policy-driven orchestration layer, while Q-Pathformer provides execution-side mechanisms for 
dataset grouping, adaptive weighting, and model training. The UGCCMT model further 
introduces a structured method for partitioning data into clusters, assigning colour-coded 
categories, encoding metadata into cryptographic salts, and shaping training behavior through 
weighted measures.

9.3 Optional UGCCMT and Capsule Metadata 
When Q-Pathformer or a similar execution environment is used, the Dataset Passport may 
include an optional execution extension. This extension records implementation-specific 
metadata needed by the downstream training or runtime system. 
In the case of Q-Pathformer, optional metadata may include: 
• UGCCMT grouping identifiers 
• colour-code classification 
• measure profiles 
• capsule identifiers 
• staged training hints 
• synthetic or runtime preparation flags 
The UGCCMT model defines six stages— Unit, Group, Colour, Code, Measure, and Train— which 
together support partitioning, risk classification, metadata encoding, and training-sensitive key 
derivation. These stages can be represented as optional metadata fields attached to a passport 
without altering the passport’s governance semantics. 
Similarly, capsule pipeline metadata may describe how a dataset is organized into reproducible 
training units for staged execution. Q-Pathformer materials describe capsules as modular 
training units containing curated data, deterministic labeling, semantic enrichment, and 
embedded configuration metadata. 
These metadata fields are therefore execution-supporting, not governance-defining.

9.4 Execution Profiles in the Dataset Passport 
To preserve interoperability, the Dataset Passport should distinguish between: 
• core governance fields, which are always present, and 
• optional execution fields, which appear only when required by the target environment. 
Core governance fields typically include: 
• dataset identity 
• provenance anchors 
• lifecycle state 
• authorization scope 
• lineage references 
• containment and promotion status 
Optional execution fields may include: 
• execution environment identifier 
• clustering or grouping metadata 
• training-stage indicators 
• capsule pipeline references 
• model-specific routing hints 
This separation allows the same passport structure to support both governance-only workflows 
and execution-aware workflows. A dataset may therefore remain fully valid within the 
onboarding framework even if no execution metadata is present.

9.5 Separation of Governance and Execution Authority 
A key principle of this framework is the separation between governance authority and 
execution behavior. 
Execution environments may consume dataset passports, organize data into training structures, 
and process optional metadata for clustering or staged learning. However, they do not 
independently determine: 
• whether a dataset is authorized for durable training, 
• whether a dataset may be used externally, 
• whether a dataset has been promoted into State 1, or 
• whether a dataset has achieved any trust, assurance, or compliance status.

Page | 36

These determinations remain external to the execution environment and must be governed 
through the lifecycle and authorization controls defined earlier in this document. 
This separation is particularly important where advanced execution systems introduce 
cryptographic provenance encoding, synthetic generation, or staged training pipelines. Such 
mechanisms may improve traceability or training discipline, but they do not alter the 
governance status of the underlying dataset.

9.6 Controlled Interoperability 
The purpose of optional execution environments is not to collapse governance into training 
logic, but to allow controlled interoperability between the two. 
Under this model, governance artifacts and dataset passports establish what may be used, 
under what conditions, and in which lifecycle state. Execution environments then consume 
those declarations and apply them within training or runtime contexts. 
This approach allows organizations to support a variety of deployment patterns, including: 
• governance-only onboarding workflows 
• internal training pipelines 
• Q-Pathformer-compatible capsule workflows 
• future architectures not yet defined 
As a result, the onboarding framework remains stable even as execution systems evolve.

Dataset passports and lineage records do not certify dataset quality, completeness, or 
correctness. 
Recording a dataset within the onboarding framework does not imply that the dataset has been

the scope of this document.

oversight.

11.2 Dataset Conversion 
Once artifacts are ingested, the implementation may perform a dataset conversion step. 
During conversion, structured signals contained within artifacts are extracted and organized 
into machine-readable dataset structures. These signals may include scenario descriptions, 
analytical observations, governance annotations, or other structured information relevant to 
model training. 
The conversion process should preserve provenance anchors by linking dataset records to their 
originating artifacts. This linkage allows dataset lineage to remain visible even after 
transformation into training-ready structures. 
Conversion tools may produce provisional datasets that enter the lifecycle pipeline as State 3 
datasets.

• lifecycle state 
• authorization scope 
• lineage references 
Passport generation provides the governance context required for routing decisions within the 
lifecycle model. 
Implementations may automate passport creation during dataset conversion so that each 
dataset unit is immediately associated with its governance metadata.

11.4 Lifecycle Routing 
After passport generation, datasets are routed according to the lifecycle rules defined earlier in

Page | 41

In most cases, newly created datasets will be routed to State 3, where they remain under 
containment while supporting runtime reasoning, simulation, or synthetic dataset generation. 
Datasets may later move into State 2 during validation or governance review processes. 
Routing decisions may be informed by attributes recorded in the Dataset Passport, including 
authorization scope and lineage relationships. 
Lifecycle routing mechanisms ensure that provisional datasets do not automatically become 
durable training corpora.

11.5 Authorization Filtering 
Before datasets become eligible for durable training use, implementations should perform 
authorization filtering. 
Authorization filtering ensures that dataset elements exceeding their permitted usage scope 
are removed or restricted. This process helps enforce governance policies and prevents 
unauthorized signals from entering persistent training datasets. 
Filtering decisions should be guided by the authorization scope recorded in the Dataset 
Passport. If dataset elements conflict with governance constraints, those elements must be 
excluded from the dataset version considered for promotion. 
Authorization filtering therefore acts as the final containment mechanism before datasets 
move toward durable training use.

12.2 Signal Extraction Example 
The dataset signals recorded in the passport originate from the module records contained 
within the freeze package. 
These records capture structured reasoning signals observed during governance stress 
simulations. Examples of captured signals include: 
• scenario seeds describing operational conditions 
• stressors such as time pressure or conflicting telemetry 
• fragility points identifying governance boundary drift 
• uncertainty notes documenting interpretive limits 
• escalation triggers identifying governance intervention points. 
These signals do not represent governance decisions. Instead, they document reasoning 
conditions and interpretive signals that may later be used for exploratory learning, runtime 
reasoning, or synthetic dataset generation. 
The passport therefore preserves the contextual meaning of the signals while preventing their 
automatic promotion into durable training datasets.

13.7 Reference Implementations and Release Tiers 
Future releases associated with the Access-PoD research program may include additional 
implementation artifacts and reference environments supporting the governed dataset lifecycle 
model. 
These releases may include research and educational reference implementations, strategic 
governance tooling, SPDX-aligned operational models, and multimodal training environments 
supporting modular agent architectures. 
Examples under exploration include multimodal agent frameworks with configurations such as 
16-agent, 64-agent, and 144-agent architectures, as well as associated training code and model 
weight artifacts distributed through separate repositories or releases. 
These implementations remain optional and do not alter the governance semantics defined in 
this document.

Closing Perspective 
The framework presented in this document represents the next step in the evolution of the 
Access-PoD research series. Version A established the conceptual foundation for engineering 
trust through runtime evidence, simulation-driven governance, and telemetry-derived 
assurance. Version B introduced an optional architecture illustration demonstrating how 
governance controls may interact with execution environments without altering the model-
agnostic nature of the framework. Version C extended this foundation by defining an 
onboarding and operational transition discipline designed to manage uncertainty as AI systems 
move from experimental contexts into controlled runtime governance. 
This report builds on those foundations by introducing a structured mechanism for 
transforming governance artifacts into machine-readable datasets through the Dataset 
Passport and lifecycle routing model. Together, these publications describe a coherent 
governance progression: from conceptual trust engineering, to architecture-aware governance, 
to operational onboarding discipline, and finally to governed dataset lifecycle management.

Status: Public Review Draft (Standards Exploration) 
Author: Anthony Siljeg 
Affiliation: Alnotrea Labs / Policy of Developments - Access PoD Initiative. 
Document Scope 
This technical report defines an execution-layer framework for tiered model signal exchange, 
controlled maturity routing, and governance-constrained dataset formation in AI training systems. 
The report explains how signal interactions across model classes can be captured, structured, 
routed, packaged, frozen, and prepared for training within lifecycle-controlled environments. 
It establishes governance-aware execution semantics, maturity-routing boundaries, and dataset 
formation controls, but does not prescribe a single machine learning architecture, model family, 
training pipeline, or deployment environment. 
Execution systems such as Q-Pathformer may consume lifecycle-governed datasets produced under 
this framework, but such systems do not define governance authority within the Access-PoD model. 
This document extends the governance framework established in APOD-TR-002 (Version A), the 
architecture illustration described in APOD-TR-003 (Version B), the onboarding discipline defined in 
APOD-TR-004 (Version C), and the dataset lifecycle and passport model defined in APOD-TR-007. It 
introduces the execution-layer routing model for governed signal exchange, controlled maturity 
progression, and dataset formation in AI training environments.

In the present Q-Pathformer release, runtime signal generation uses a 20B-class model (gpt-oss:20b), and, after explicit promotion into STATE_1, training preparation uses a 1.1B local LoRA base (TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0).

New source signals and newly onboarded external artifacts enter under STATE_3 containment by default; controlled candidate packages may be handled in STATE_2 for review, while STATE_1 is reserved for promoted datasets prepared for governed training use.

Execution environments may implement signal capture, routing, and dataset formation mechanisms without inheriting governance authority.

In the present release, this framework is realized across three governed dataset formation paths: a TR corpus and reference path, an Access-Mode ID_2 to ID_3 canonical lifecycle path, and an external or custom dataset adapter path.

Abstract 
This technical report extends the governed dataset lifecycle framework defined in APOD-TR-
007 by introducing a tier-aware signal interaction model for AI training environments 
operating across multiple model classes. 
The report defines a structured execution model for controlled signal exchange between 
model tiers. In the present Q-Pathformer release, runtime signal generation uses a 20B-class 
model (gpt-oss:20b), and, after explicit promotion into STATE_1, training preparation uses a 
1.1B local LoRA base (TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0). New source signals and newly 
onboarded external artifacts enter under STATE_3 containment by default; controlled 
candidate packages may be handled in STATE_2 for review, while STATE_1 is reserved for 
promoted datasets prepared for governed training use. The active Q-Pathformer GitHub 
release branches are the reference baseline (reference_sparse_e08 agents released) and 
the enterprise target (grouped_sparse_e64 agents released). Governance schemas 
distinguish enterprise routing ranges (12B–14B) from optional strategic ranges (24B–30B), 
while strategic profiles such as fused_sparse_e144 remain internal architectural references 
for future API-mediated signal access rather than required release components. 
Signal interactions are represented through a structured interaction-role model in which 
signals generated by one system may be interpreted, filtered, and transformed by another 
into governed dataset artifacts. These roles are contextual to each interaction and do not 
imply hierarchy, authority, or a trust gradient between model tiers. 
All cross-tier signals are treated as provisional artifacts and remain subject to lifecycle 
containment as defined in APOD-TR-007. Signals and newly onboarded external artifacts are 
assigned to STATE_3 by default and may support runtime reasoning, synthetic dataset 
generation, or exploratory analysis. STATE_2 provides the controlled validation and 
convergence layer for candidate datasets, while progression to STATE_1 requires explicit 
validation, authorization filtering, issuance of a governed dataset passport, and promotion 
under governed review.

The architecture defines a structured transformation pipeline: 
runtime signal capture

→ prepared freeze input (freeze-ready artifact record)

Each stage introduces additional structure and governance control. 
Key characteristics of this pipeline: 
• signals are progressively structured into dataset records 
• candidate datasets are filtered and validated before admission 
• dataset packages preserve: 
o dataset content, 
o governance artifacts, 
o and traceability references 
• pre-freeze preparation normalizes governance metadata 
• freeze produces an inspection-ready artifact snapshot 
The pipeline ensures that dataset evolution is: 
• explicit, 
• traceable, 
• and governed at each stage.

Page | 28

3.6 Dataset Packaging and Freeze Integration 
The architecture integrates dataset packaging and freeze as explicit stages. 
Pre-freeze produces a prepared freeze manifest and a prepared freeze input record, which 
together deﬁne the exact artifact set consumed by the freeze boundary. 
Dataset packaging produces: 
• a structured dataset package (ID_2 snapshot) 
• including: 
o dataset records, 
o manifest, 
o passport, 
o routing, 
o authorization, 
o and lineage artifacts 
Freeze transforms this package into: 
• a stable, inspection-ready snapshot under ID_3 posture 
The freeze output includes: 
• a preserved dataset package snapshot 
• inspection-oriented canonical artifacts 
• freeze evidence records 
• and a freeze manifest binding all components 
This structure ensures that: 
• dataset content remains unchanged during freeze, 
• governance artifacts remain explicit, 
• and inspection is supported without altering dataset semantics.

3.7 Execution-Agnostic Design

The architecture does not depend on: 
• specific model implementations, 
• training frameworks, 
• or deployment environments.

Enterprise-tier models represent the primary runtime systems within the TR-008 
architecture. 
Typical characteristics include: 
• parameter class in the range of 12B–14B, 
• local or enterprise-managed deployment, 
• direct interaction with runtime environments, 
• and responsibility for signal capture and dataset structuring. 
Enterprise-tier models are responsible for: 
• generating structured signals from runtime interactions, 
• interpreting signals produced by other systems, 
• filtering and organizing signals into candidate dataset artifacts, 
• and operating under lifecycle containment constraints. 
Enterprise-tier models operate under: 
• ID_2 (operational reasoning posture), 
• and produce signals that are exploratory, conditional, and non-authoritative.

Page | 31

4.3 Strategic-Tier Models 
Strategic-tier models represent higher-capacity internal or future-facing reference systems 
that may be invoked under controlled conditions when enabled. 
Typical characteristics include: 
• larger parameter classes (e.g., 24B–30B or higher), 
• optional, indirect, or API-mediated invocation, 
• and use for internal signal amplification, synthesis, or extended reasoning under 
containment. 
When enabled, strategic-tier models may: 
• generate structured reasoning signals, 
• produce alternative interpretations, 
• and contribute to internal scenario exploration under containment. 
Any resulting signals are treated as: 
• upstream signal artifacts, 
• non-authoritative and subject to governance constraints, 
• and subject to lifecycle routing and validation by enterprise-tier controls. 
Within the present release, strategic-tier models do not: 
• define governance outcomes, 
• operate as required release components or override enterprise-tier systems, 
• or transfer authority to downstream processes.

generation and dataset formation.

Within this model: 
• signal originators generate structured reasoning outputs, 
• signal interpreters transform those outputs into governed dataset artifacts.

4.5 Capability vs Authority Separation 
A core principle of TR-008 is the separation of capability and authority. 
Model capability refers to: 
• computational capacity, 
• reasoning complexity, 
• and representational power. 
Authority refers to: 
• governance decision-making, 
• authorization of dataset use, 
• and determination of correctness or adequacy. 
Within this architecture: 
• Capability does not imply authority. 
• and higher-capacity models do not possess elevated governance status. 
All outputs produced by any model tier are: 
• treated as signals, 
• subject to validation, 
• and governed through lifecycle and authorization mechanisms.

• or a delegation of authority.

• subject to lifecycle containment, 
• and governed externally to the execution system.

Interaction between model tiers is strictly controlled. 
All cross-tier interaction must occur through: 
• structured signal artifacts, 
• dataset records, 
• and governance-controlled routing.

• shared memory, 
• implicit state transfer, 
• or direct model-to-model control 
are not permitted within this architecture.

• all interactions are traceable, 
• signals remain inspectable, 
• and governance controls can be applied consistently.

inherits authority, trust, or correctness from another system through interaction.

Within TR-008, the signal is the primary system artifact from which downstream dataset

• structured summaries, 
• contextual observations,

5.8 Lineage and Traceability Requirements 
Signal records must support traceability across transformation stages. 
At minimum, a signal should preserve enough information to allow later reconstruction of: 
• where the signal originated, 
• which session or interaction produced it, 
• which model role generated it, 
• what governance flags applied at capture, 
• and how it was later transformed into dataset artifacts. 
Where signals contribute to candidate dataset formation, lineage continuity should be 
preserved through references into: 
• candidate manifests, 
• dataset passports, 
• routing records, 
• and lineage records. 
This aligns with TR-007’s treatment of lineage as informative traceability documentation 
rather than as a signal of approval or trust.

5.9 Non-Authoritative Signal Constraints 
TR-008 requires that signal records preserve explicit non-authoritative constraints. 
The origin of a signal does not confer authority. Signals produced by higher-capacity systems 
must be treated identically to all other signals within the lifecycle and routing model.

Page | 40

A signal record shall not be interpreted as: 
• a governance decision, 
• a dataset approval, 
• a promotion event, 
• or a compliance determination. 
To preserve this boundary, signal records should be structured and labeled so that: 
• signals remain distinguishable from dataset passports, 
• execution metadata remains distinguishable from governance metadata, 
• and provisional records remain distinguishable from frozen artifacts. 
This protects the principle that signals are execution artifacts only.

6. Signal Lifecycle and Dataset State Mapping 
6.1 Purpose of Lifecycle Mapping 
This section defines how captured signal records are mapped into governed dataset lifecycle 
states. 
The purpose of lifecycle mapping is to: 
• prevent uncontrolled transformation of signals into training datasets, 
• preserve dataset containment and authorization boundaries, 
• ensure traceable progression from signal to dataset artifact, 
• and enforce governance constraints prior to any dataset promotion. 
Signal lifecycle mapping provides the operational bridge between:

6.2 Signal-to-Dataset Transformation Boundary 
Signals represent the earliest structured form of AI-assisted reasoning outputs. 
At the point of capture: 
• signals are treated as provisional artifacts, 
• signals are not considered datasets, 
• and signals must not be used directly for training or durable storage. 
Transformation into dataset artifacts occurs only through: 
• structured conversion, 
• governance validation, 
• and lifecycle-aware routing. 
This boundary ensures that: 
• model outputs do not bypass governance controls, 
• dataset formation is explicit and traceable, 
• and dataset artifacts retain linkage to their originating signals.

All captured signals are assigned to a provisional lifecycle state. 
Within TR-008, this corresponds to: 
STATE_3 — runtime / synthetic dataset layer 
Signals entering STATE_3 are: 
• context-bound, 
• non-authoritative and subject to governance constraints, 
• and intended for runtime reasoning or synthetic dataset preparation. 
This aligns with dataset lifecycle behavior where newly onboarded artifacts remain under 
containment and are not eligible for durable training use. 
Example characteristics of STATE_3 artifacts include:

Page | 42

• signals derived from ID_2 operational reasoning 
• datasets generated from ID_3 frozen artifacts but not yet validated 
• exploratory or scenario-based reasoning outputs 
STATE_3 is therefore the default entry point for all signals.

• governance-first,

Routing in TR-008 follows a strict governance-first principle. 
Routing decisions must not be influenced by the perceived capability, origin, or interaction 
role of a signal-producing system. 
This means: 
• governance constraints are evaluated before signal quality or maturity, 
• authorization is evaluated before validation eligibility, 
• and lifecycle state transitions are blocked unless all conditions are satisfied. 
Routing must not: 
• infer readiness from signal structure, 
• infer authority from model capability, 
• or infer promotion eligibility from maturity classification.

Page | 48

The default routing outcome is: 
HOLD_IN_STATE_3 
This conservative default ensures that: 
• signals remain contained, 
• uncertainty is preserved, 
• and governance conditions are not bypassed.

7.3 Deterministic Routing Model 
Routing decisions must be deterministic. 
For any given signal record: 
• the same inputs must produce the same routing outcome, 
• evaluation order must not change, 
• and routing decisions must be reproducible. 
Routing inputs include: 
• signal record (schema-compliant) 
• governance flags 
• authorization block 
• validation indicators 
• lifecycle fields 
• diagnostic metrics and maturity classification 
Routing outputs include: 
• lifecycle decision (e.g., HOLD, SEND_TO_STATE_2, REJECT) 
• updated lifecycle fields 
• routing reason codes 
• routing log record 
Routing must remain: 
• model-agnostic 
• execution-independent 
• and fully auditable

7.4 Fixed Gate Evaluation Order

Page | 49

Routing must follow a fixed, ordered evaluation sequence. 
No gate may be skipped or reordered. 
Gate A — Structural Admission 
Checks: 
• schema validity 
• required fields present 
• lifecycle initialized (STATE_3) 
• model metadata present 
Failure outcome: 
REJECT_SIGNAL

Gate B — Governance Constraint Check 
Checks: 
• governance flags present 
• signal remains provisional and non-authoritative 
• no blocking governance condition 
Failure outcome: 
HOLD_IN_STATE_3 or REJECT_SIGNAL

• ambiguity within acceptable bounds 
• stability sufficient for evaluation

• eligible_for_state_2 = true 
• routing_decision = SEND_TO_STATE_2_REVIEW

This gate sequence ensures that: 
• governance overrides all other signals, 
• authorization precedes validation, 
• and maturity remains advisory only.

7.5 Routing Outcomes 
Routing decisions are constrained to a finite set of outcomes: 
• HOLD_IN_STATE_3 
• SEND_TO_STATE_2_REVIEW 
• RETURN_TO_STATE_3 
• REJECT_SIGNAL

Page | 51

• HOLD_IN_STATE_3 is the default 
• SEND_TO_STATE_2 requires full gate satisfaction 
• RETURN_TO_STATE_3 applies when validation fails or context changes 
• REJECT_SIGNAL applies only for structural or governance failure 
All routing outcomes must be: 
• explicitly recorded 
• accompanied by reason codes 
• traceable through routing logs

7.6 Authorization and Validation Separation 
Routing enforces strict separation between: 
• authorization 
• validation 
• and signal maturity 
Key constraints: 
• Validation does not imply authorization. 
• Maturity does not imply readiness. 
• Review does not imply permission. 
For example: 
• signals may be eligible for validation 
• but still blocked from training due to authorization restrictions 
• and require human review before promotion 
This separation ensures that: 
• dataset formation remains controlled, 
• lifecycle progression is governed, 
• and training eligibility is not inferred implicitly.

7.7 Governance Flag Enforcement 
Governance flags act as hard constraints on routing behavior. 
Typical flags include: 
• provisional

Page | 52

• context_bound 
• requires_validation 
• promotion_blocked 
Rules: 
• governance flags override maturity and metrics 
• promotion_blocked must default to true 
• routing must check flags before evaluating signal quality 
If governance conditions are not satisfied: 
• routing must halt progression 
• or reject the signal 
This ensures the following: 
• Signals remain non-authoritative. 
• dataset formation remains controlled, 
• and lifecycle constraints are preserved.

7.8 Cross-Tier Routing Constraints 
Signals originating from cross-tier interaction must follow the same routing rules. 
Additional constraints include: 
• strategic-tier signals must be interpreted by enterprise-tier before routing 
• all cross-tier outputs remain provisional 
• no signal inherits authority from model size 
Routing must enforce: 
• initiator and amplifier traceability 
• structured interpretation before artifact creation 
• lifecycle containment identical to single-tier signals 
This prevents: 
• implicit authority transfer 
• and uncontrolled influence of higher-capacity models

7.9 Escalation Policy (Enterprise → Strategic)

Page | 53

TR-008 permits controlled escalation from enterprise-tier execution to optional strategic-
tier reference services when such services are enabled. 
Escalation may occur when: 
• ambiguity is high 
• signal coherence is low 
• alternative reasoning paths are required 
• or explicit escalation is requested through controlled configuration 
Rules: 
• enterprise-tier initiates escalation 
• strategic-tier produces candidate signals only 
• outputs must return to enterprise-tier for structuring 
• all outputs remain in STATE_3 unless separately validated and promoted under 
lifecycle rules 
Within the present release, escalation is: 
• explicit, 
• reversible, 
• non-authoritative and subject to governance constraints, 
and optional to successful execution of the released paths. 
• This ensures that strategic-tier services act only as internal signal amplifiers or future 
API reference points, 
• not decision-makers or required release components.

7.10 Routing Logs and Traceability 
All routing decisions must be recorded. 
A routing log must include: 
• signal_id 
• source_state 
• target_state 
• routing decision 
• reason code 
• timestamp 
Optional fields may include: 
• model parameter class

Page | 54

• interaction type 
• escalation usage 
Routing logs must be: 
• append-only 
• immutable 
• and fully traceable 
This supports: 
• auditability 
• lifecycle reconstruction 
• and governance oversight

7.11 Failure Handling and Conservative Defaults 
Routing must implement conservative failure handling. 
Rules: 
• invalid signal → REJECT 
• missing fields → REJECT 
• authorization missing → HOLD 
• validation uncertain → HOLD 
• governance conflict → HOLD or REJECT 
When uncertainty exists: 
do not promote 
This ensures: 
• lifecycle integrity 
• prevention of silent failure 
• and controlled dataset evolution

7.12 Routing Invariants 
The routing system enforces the following invariants: 
• governance overrides maturity 
• authorization overrides validation 
• signals remain provisional by default

Page | 55

• no automatic promotion to STATE_1 
• model capability does not affect authority 
• all transitions are explicit and logged 
These invariants ensure that: 
• routing remains governance-first, 
• dataset progression remains controlled, 
• and system behavior remains interpretable.

interact with this architecture. 
Section 8 defines: 
• signal emission from runtime systems 
• execution flow and orchestration 
• model endpoint abstraction 
• and integration with local and remote environments

8. Runtime Integration 
8.1 Purpose of Runtime Integration 
This section defines how runtime systems generate, structure, and emit signals within the 
TR-008 architecture. 
The runtime layer is responsible for: 
• executing model interactions, 
• capturing outputs as structured signal records, 
• attaching execution and model metadata, 
• and preparing signals for routing and lifecycle processing. 
Runtime integration provides the operational entry point into the governed dataset 
lifecycle.

It does not determine governance authority, assign dataset authorization, or perform 
lifecycle promotion.

All runtime outputs remain:

Page | 56

• ID_2 artifacts, 
• provisional, 
• and subject to governance constraints.

8.2 Signal Emission from Runtime Systems 
Runtime systems must emit all outputs as structured signal records. 
Signal emission must follow a consistent transformation pipeline: 
prompt input 
→ model resolution 
→ enterprise-tier execution 
→ (optional) strategic-tier amplification 
→ enterprise-tier interpretation and structuring 
→ metric scoring and maturity classification 
→ JSON schema binding 
→ validation 
→ artifact storage

Drift detection identifies changes in model behavior over time.

Structural Drift 
• schema violations 
• missing required fields 
• inconsistent formatting 
Behavioral Drift 
• increased ambiguity 
• loss of structured discipline 
• unstable outputs

• lifecycle misassignment 
• emergence of authority-like language 
Drift detection is based on: 
• baseline comparison 
• threshold evaluation 
• anomaly detection 
Drift signals must be: 
• recorded 
• traceable 
• and reviewable

• thresholds are configurable

10.9 Revocation Triggers 
Revocation is triggered when: 
• critical drift is detected 
• structural failure exceeds acceptable limits 
• governance violations occur 
• unexpected behavior patterns emerge 
Revocation conditions must be: 
• explicit 
• recorded 
• and reviewable 
Revocation is a governance action, not an automated conclusion.

10.10 Revocation and Rollback Actions

Page | 76

When revocation is required: 
• the affected model version is disabled 
• the system reverts to a previous stable version 
• the revocation event is recorded 
• the failed model is preserved for analysis 
Rules: 
• no silent rollback 
• revoked models must not be reused 
• all actions must be traceable 
Rollback must: 
• restore prior behavior 
• preserve lineage 
• and maintain auditability

10.11 Continuous Evaluation Loop 
Evaluation operates as a continuous loop: 
baseline 
→ dataset formation 
→ model adaptation 
→ evaluation 
→ comparison 
→ decision (retain / rollback / revise) 
Rules: 
• evaluation must follow every model update 
• no model progresses without evaluation 
• decisions must be explicit 
• conservative action is the default 
This loop ensures that: 
• model evolution remains controlled 
• dataset impact is measurable 
• and governance constraints are preserved

10.12 Governance Safeguards

Page | 77

The evaluation system must enforce: 
• evaluation does not create authority 
• Passing evaluation does not imply approval. 
• outputs remain ID_2 signals 
• lifecycle rules cannot be overridden 
Evaluation must not: 
• promote datasets 
• authorize training 
• or alter governance status 
This maintains separation between: 
• execution 
• evaluation 
• and governance authority

12. Dataset Freeze Boundary (ID_3 Packaging and Archive Freeze) 
12.1 Purpose of the Freeze Boundary 
This section defines the dataset freeze boundary as applied within the Q-Pathformer 
execution environment. 
The freeze boundary represents the transition from a governed dataset package assembled 
under operational reasoning conditions to a stable, inspection-ready artifact prepared for 
external interpretation. 
This boundary is aligned with: 
• the inspection posture defined in Access-Mode ID_3, 
• the artifact lifecycle clarification described in APOD-TR-006-E.2, and 
• the dataset containment and lifecycle routing model defined in APOD-TR-007. 
The freeze boundary represents the final stage of the execution pipeline defined in this 
report, following: 
• signal capture, 
• dataset formation, 
• dataset packaging, 
• and pre-freeze preparation. 
The purpose of the freeze boundary is to: 
• preserve dataset structure and governance context as a fixed snapshot, 
• ensure deterministic integrity through cryptographic hashing, 
• enable inspection and review without altering dataset content or semantics, and 
• prevent implicit authority or approval from being inferred from dataset 
completeness.

12.2 Freeze as an Artifact State Transition 
The freeze operation is an explicit artifact-state transition. 
Dataset packages assembled under ID_2 operational reasoning posture remain non-
inspectable until explicitly transitioned to ID_3 through the freeze boundary. 
A dataset is considered frozen only when: 
• it is prepared under ID_3 inspection posture, 
• the artifact set is treated as issued for review, 
• and further modification is suspended or versioned. 
Freezing is a deliberate act and must not occur implicitly. 
In accordance with APOD-TR-006-E.2: 
• freezing indicates that an artifact set is stable enough for inspection, 
• but does not imply correctness, adequacy, compliance, or approval. 
The freeze boundary therefore represents a transition in artifact state, not a change in 
governance authority or dataset trust status.

12.3 Relationship to Dataset Lifecycle States 
The freeze boundary operates within the dataset lifecycle model defined in APOD-TR-007. 
In this model: 
• datasets assembled through signal capture and candidate formation ordinarily begin 
within STATE_3, 
• STATE_3 datasets are provisional, context-bound, and governed by containment 
until review and promotion occur, 
• and datasets must not be treated as durable training assets without explicit 
promotion. 
Freezing a provisional STATE_3 artifact does not promote a dataset to STATE_1. 
Separately: 
• the release also permits downstream STATE_1 handoff and freeze operations after 
explicit promotion; these do not make STATE_1 an entry state. 
• The freeze operation preserves a stable snapshot appropriate to the lifecycle state 
being frozen. 
This distinction ensures that:

Page | 87

• Dataset existence does not imply authorization for training use. 
• Inspection readiness does not imply dataset maturity or approval.

A dataset may be frozen only when a complete set of freeze inputs is present.

prior to hashing and freeze execution.

• module-level canonical records

• human-readable declaration of freeze scope and limitations

12.5 Frozen Package Structure 
The freeze process produces a structured artifact set composed of distinct layers: 
frozen_package_root/ 
├── dataset_package_snapshot/ (ID_2 dataset package snapshot) 
├── canonical_artifacts/ (ID_3 inspection artifacts) 
├── freeze_evidence/ (freeze note and hash manifests) 
└── freeze_manifest.json 
Each layer serves a distinct purpose: 
dataset package snapshot 
• contains an exact copy of the dataset package assembled under ID_2 
• preserves dataset content and governance artifacts without modification 
• represents the original ID_2 dataset package snapshot preserved under the ID_3 
freeze boundary 
canonical artifacts 
• contains inspection-oriented canonical artifacts 
• supports reviewer interpretation and traceability 
freeze evidence 
• contains: 
o expected hash definitions 
o computed hash manifest 
o freeze declaration note 
freeze_manifest.json 
• binds the freeze event to: 
o source package 
o artifact locations 
o hash records 
o and freeze posture

Page | 89

The frozen package is derived from the prepared freeze input record, not directly from the 
original package assembly location. 
This separation ensures that: 
• runtime dataset content, 
• inspection artifacts, 
• and integrity evidence 
remain clearly distinguishable.

The Working-PoD lifecycle defines a separation between:

ready.

• explicit freeze under ID_3,

13.6 Prevention of Authority Inflation 
A key purpose of the Working-PoD lifecycle is to prevent the misinterpretation of artifact 
completeness as authority. 
TR-008 reinforces this by ensuring that: 
• structured datasets do not imply correctness, 
• populated artifacts do not imply readiness, 
• frozen artifacts do not imply approval or compliance. 
Even when artifacts are: 
• fully structured, 
• validated, 
• and frozen, 
they remain: 
• non-authoritative and subject to governance constraints, 
• subject to challenge, 
• and dependent on human interpretation. 
This prevents: 
• learning artifacts from being treated as conclusions, 
• operational artifacts from being treated as validated outcomes,

Page | 95

• and inspection artifacts from being treated as endorsements.

• Signal capture does not imply progression beyond draft. 
• Dataset structuring does not imply inspection readiness. 
• freeze must be explicitly declared 
Each transition must be accompanied by: 
• a clear Access-Mode context, 
• a statement of intended use, 
• and explicit limitation or scope declarations. 
Silent transitions — particularly from populated to frozen — must be avoided.

B.4 Adapter Ingestion Process 
Adapter ingestion performs the following operations: 
1. Source Classification 
o identify artifact type 
o detect originating posture (ID_1 / ID_2 / ID_3 where applicable) 
o determine structural completeness

Page | 109

2. Schema Mapping and Normalization 
o convert input into canonical dataset-compatible structure 
o align fields to signal or dataset schema 
o enforce minimal structural requirements 
3. Provenance Preservation 
o attach source references 
o retain canonical artifact identifiers where available 
o bind lineage anchors to input records 
4. Authorization Context Handling 
o inherit authorization scope where defined 
o otherwise default to restricted containment posture 
o prevent implicit expansion of usage rights 
5. Lifecycle Initialization 
o assign default lifecycle state: 
 STATE_3 — provisional dataset layer 
• attach lifecycle flags and routing-ready metadata

B.5 Default Routing Outcome 
All ingested artifacts must default to: 
 STATE_3 (Runtime / Synthetic Dataset Layer) 
This ensures alignment with the dataset containment principle defined in TR-007, where 
newly onboarded datasets remain provisional and not eligible for durable training use 
without explicit promotion. 
No artifact may: 
• bypass lifecycle entry, 
• enter STATE_1 directly, or 
• be treated as training-ready without validation and authorization.

Following ingestion: 
• artifacts may be transformed into signal records, or 
• signals may be extracted directly from structured inputs 
All downstream processing must:

Page | 110

• conform to the signal schema defined in Section 5, 
• preserve governance flags, 
• and remain traceable to original sources.

Adapter ingestion must preserve the following invariants:

Document Scope 
This document deﬁnes a standards-facing interpretation of the Compliance Star Certiﬁcate 
(CSC) within the Q-Pathformer Enterprise v1.0 release.

It explains how CSC, as deﬁned in the Access-PoD Version A framework (APOD-TR-002), is 
instantiated through execution-bound evidence, including runtime signals, lifecycle-governed 
dataset artifacts, evaluation outputs, and sector-speciﬁc proﬁles.

The document establishes how CSC should be interpreted when expressed as session-scoped 
and run-scoped artifacts derived from bounded evidence windows, while remaining part of a 
continuous, telemetry-derived assurance model.

This document does not redeﬁne CSC scoring logic, governance authority, or lifecycle 
semantics. It does not introduce certiﬁcation, compliance determination, or regulatory 
approval mechanisms.

Instead, it provides:

• a deﬁnition of CSC as an execution-bound assurance artifact, 
• an interpretation framework for reading CSC outputs in live systems, 
• a description of the three-layer evidence model (execution, governance, sector), 
• a characterization of sparse-but-gated metric coverage and conﬁdence, 
• and a statement of current limitations and future maturity pathways.
